articles.title: Who Is Russia’s New Ambassador to North Korea?
articles.full_text:
What can Andrei Podelyshev’s appointment tell us about North Korea-Russia relations?
Shortly after his arrival in Pyongyang, Russian Ambassador to North Korea Andrei Podelyshev pays respects at the memorial honoring North Korean troops killed fighting alongside Russian forces, Sep. 26, 2026.
Russia has finally filled the ambassadorial post in Pyongyang, which had sat vacant for nearly eight months. Under a decree signed by President Vladimir Putin on July 28, career diplomat Andrei Podelyshev – at the time, Russia’s ambassador to Nigeria, a post he had held since December 2024 – was named the new ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. A companion decree released him from his Nigerian posting the same day.
Podelyshev arrived in Pyongyang nearly two months later, on September 26, together with his wife, aboard a direct Nordwind flight from Moscow. According to the Russian Embassy and TASS, he headed straight from the airport to the Soviet-era Liberation Monument to pay tribute to fallen Red Army soldiers, before visiting Pyongyang’s newly built memorial complex for North Korean troops killed fighting alongside Russian forces in Kursk.
Podelyshev is, on paper, one of the more genuinely “Korea-literate” diplomats Moscow could have sent. He graduated from MGIMO (the Moscow State Institute of International Relations) in 1984 and joined the Soviet Foreign Ministry that same year. He speaks both English and Korean, and over his career he has served at the Soviet embassy in Pyongyang itself, as well as at Russian missions in South Korea and the United States.
What stands out, though, is the decade he spent away from Asia desks entirely. From 2005 to 2015, Podelyshev was deputy director of the Consular Department of the Russian Foreign Ministry, the branch of the ministry responsible for visas, citizenship matters, and the movement of foreign nationals in and out of Russia.
That background is not a minor biographical footnote. Consular policy has become one of the most sensitive, and most scrutinized, levers of the entire North Korea-Russia relationship. Since 2022, Russian consular services have issued tens of thousands of visas to North Korean citizens, the overwhelming majority formally classified as “educational” visas. 
According to Russia’s own data, the number of visas issued to North Koreans jumped from 9,239 in 2024 to 36,413 in 2025, with 35,849 of them, over 98 percent, nominally for education. Investigations by NK Pro and others have shown that these “student” visas are routinely used by Russian firms to bring in North Korean laborers while sidestepping United Nations Security Council Resolution 2375, which bars U.N. member states from issuing work permits to North Korean nationals.
The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, an 11-country group tracking sanctions evasion, went further in a report released September 16, 2026, stating, “The Russian government has created a student visa scheme to camouflage North Korean laborers in Russia as students,” including workers employed in drone manufacturing at Russian defense-industrial sites such as the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan The report estimates that 15,000 to 30,000 North Korean laborers were working in Russia by the end of 2025, each generating roughly $7,500 a year in wages – up to five times what similar labor earns in China.
Sending an ambassador with nearly a decade of consular-management experience to preside over an embassy now processing this volume of visa traffic is unlikely to be a coincidence. Whether or not Podelyshev personally shaped this scheme during his 2005-2015 tenure at the Consular Department, he has strong professional grounding in the visa categories, documentation, and institutional workarounds that have made the “student visa” loophole possible in the first place.
The post of Russia’s envoy to North Korea had been empty since the death of Aleksandr Matsegora, who served as ambassador from December 2014 until December 6, 2025, when he died in Pyongyang at age 70. Matsegora, also an MGIMO graduate, held the job for just over a decade, the longest tenure of any foreign ambassador to North Korea, and was present for the relationship’s most consequential turning points, including hosting the reception marking the entry into force of the June 2024 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty.
Matsegora’s profile was that of an Asia-desk veteran who rose through the ministry’s regional bureaucracy. His successor, Podelyshev, combines an earlier Korea specialization with a mid-career detour into consular administration and, most recently, a comparatively low-profile ambassadorship in Nigeria. He is not one of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s marquee Asia strategists; he is more of a technocrat suited to managing an embassy whose day-to-day workload – handling visas, labor migration, and logistics – has expanded dramatically alongside the military relationship.
Unlike the politically weighted appointments Russia sometimes makes to signal priority, Podelyshev is not a front-rank figure in shaping strategy toward Pyongyang. His nomination reads as a bet on administrative competence, someone who can run the visa pipeline and consular relationship, at a moment when the institution-building phase may be giving way to a more routine, logistics-heavy phase of the alliance.
Podelyshev will oversee the continued evolution of the deepest North Korea-Russia alignment since the Cold War. Since the 2024 security treaty was signed, North Korea has sent more than 10,000 troops to help Russia retake Kursk, along with supplying Russia’s military with munitions and ballistic missiles. South Korean intelligence estimates that North Korea has deployed over 16,000 troops to Russia since October 2024, alongside more than 15 million artillery rounds supplied. The United States estimates that Pyongyang earned somewhere from $7.7 billion to $14.4 billion through 2025 for its military assistance to Russia. Cooperation continues, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying that North Korea is preparing to deploy another 10,000 troops to Russia.
Podelyshev’s first public act, honoring both Soviet World War II dead and North Korean Kursk casualties on the same day, signaled Moscow’s intent to frame today’s military alignment as the natural extension of a Soviet-era blood bond, rather than as a wartime marriage of convenience.
But before Podelyshev arrived, Moscow left the Pyongyang post unfilled for nearly eight months, even during the most intense period of military cooperation in the relationship’s history. The extended vacancy suggests that the strategic decisions binding the two countries are being made elsewhere — through the direct leaders’ channel and military-intelligence links, rather than through the embassy itself.

articles.title: The Geopolitics of AI in the Asia-Pacific
articles.full_text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Jouko Ahvenainen – founder and chairman of Mission Grey and serial entrepreneur in data analytics, fintech, and external intelligence – is the 528th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.” 
In what ways is artificial intelligence shaping geopolitical trends in the Asia-Pacific?
AI is increasingly connecting technology policy, national security, industrial policy, and geopolitics. Nowhere is this more visible than in the Asia-Pacific.
It is important, however, not to see the region simply through a China-U.S. lens. Taiwan is critical to advanced semiconductor manufacturing; South Korea and Japan have major positions in semiconductors, materials, and industrial technology; India is building its own AI capabilities; and Singapore and other ASEAN countries are developing their own approaches to AI infrastructure, governance, and investment.
China is particularly important because of its ability to combine technology development with hardware manufacturing, industrial scale, and rapid deployment. We already see this with electric vehicles and many other technologies: Chinese companies are increasingly selling globally, including throughout Europe despite trade frictions. AI will become another layer in this industrial and commercial expansion.
This creates a much more complex geopolitical network. Countries are asking where their compute comes from, whose models they use, where their data resides, what hardware and infrastructure they depend on, and how dependent they want to become on any single technology ecosystem.
I divide my own time between Asia, Europe, and the Americas, and one thing I see clearly is that AI development is happening in all of these regions. The differences are often in emphasis, speed, business culture, and the relationship between government and industry rather than simply in technological capability.
For businesses, these developments are no longer abstract geopolitical questions. They can quickly affect suppliers, market access, regulation, cybersecurity and investment. This is why at Mission Grey we see external intelligence becoming increasingly important: technology signals need to be understood together with political, economic, industrial, and supply chain signals.
Share your perspective on a recent comment from European technology chief Henna Virkkunen that “AI is a geopolitical weapon.”
I understand her point, and the concern behind it is real: Europe’s dependency on foreign models and infrastructure, and the leverage that dependency creates. I share that concern. But I would not describe AI itself as a weapon.
It is a general-purpose technology that is becoming strategically very important. There is a useful comparison with aviation and drone technologies. They can clearly have major military applications, but the technologies themselves are much broader than weapons. They also transform transportation, logistics, agriculture, communications, and many other areas. AI is similar, although potentially even broader in its impact.
AI can certainly be weaponized. It can strengthen military systems, intelligence capabilities, cyber operations, and information influence. Access to advanced chips, computing infrastructure, cloud services, or models can also be restricted and used as geopolitical leverage. This is where Virkkunen’s warning is most relevant, and it is a legitimate one.
But AI’s strategic importance goes much further. It will influence productivity, scientific research, industrial competitiveness, education, healthcare, and the ability to create new companies and services. Its geopolitical significance may ultimately come as much from these economic and societal effects as from direct military applications.
I would say AI is becoming a strategic capability and source of geopolitical power. That is broader, and in my view more important, than simply calling it a weapon.
What is the geopolitical impact of Asia’s AI developments on the United States and Europe?
The first impact is that Asia should no longer be viewed simply as a manufacturing base or market for Western technology. It is increasingly a source of technology, capital, standards, products, and AI ecosystems itself.
China is the most obvious example. Its strength is not only in AI models, but also in combining software with hardware, manufacturing capacity, and the ability to scale products very quickly. Its electric vehicle industry, which I mentioned earlier, shows how rapidly this can become a global commercial force. Similar dynamics can emerge around robotics, autonomous systems, and AI-enabled products.
But the broader Asian picture matters just as much. Japan and South Korea remain major technology powers, Taiwan has an exceptional position in semiconductors, India is building significant AI capabilities, and Singapore has positioned itself as an international technology and AI hub.
For the United States, maintaining leadership therefore increasingly depends not only on domestic innovation but also on partnerships and supply chains throughout Asia.
Europe faces a somewhat different challenge, but I think the common description of Europe as mainly a regulator is too simplistic. There is substantial AI innovation in Europe. France has become an important AI hub, while Sweden has a strong technology startup ecosystem, with companies such as Lovable reaching a multi-billion valuation within about two years and demonstrating how quickly new AI businesses can emerge. Both countries are also significant in defense technology.
Europe also brings another dimension to the discussion: individual control over data and technology. Concerns about data are not simply regulatory bureaucracy. People and companies are genuinely asking who controls their information, how large technology companies or governments may use it, and whether they retain the freedom to choose between different services, models and jurisdictions.
These issues will increasingly become geopolitical as well as commercial.
Examine the geopolitical stakes of pursuing technological sovereignty.
Technological sovereignty is becoming increasingly important, but the concept is often misunderstood. Sovereignty should not mean trying to manufacture everything domestically or disconnecting from global technology networks.
No major economy is genuinely independent across the entire AI stack. Advanced AI depends on an international network of semiconductor design, fabrication, memory, manufacturing equipment, cloud infrastructure, energy, data, software, and talent.
The practical objective should therefore be strategic optionality.
A country, company, or even an individual should understand which dependencies are acceptable, which are strategically critical, and where alternatives are necessary. Government systems, defense applications, and critical infrastructure naturally require particularly strong safeguards.
But sovereignty also has another level that receives less attention: the position of the user.
People and organizations increasingly depend on a small number of technology platforms for data, identity, communication, and AI. The ability to control your own data, move between services, and choose where your information is processed is therefore becoming part of technological sovereignty as well.
This is not only about Europe versus the United States or China. Different jurisdictions will make different choices concerning privacy, data access, national security, and technology governance. Users and businesses may increasingly want the ability to choose between them.
articles.summary: Insights from Jouko Ahvenainen.

articles.title: Australia Launches Bid for a UN Security Council Seat
articles.full_text:
If Australia is successful in returning to the council in 2029, it will be under significantly different circumstances than when it last held a seat.
Last week at the United Nations General Assembly, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese officially launched Australia’s campaign for a 2029-2030 non-permanent Security Council seat. Australia last held one of the non-permanent seats in 2013-2014, a period of geopolitics that now seems an entire era away, not just over a decade.
Given that we have now entered into a new, far more uncertain, period of international affairs, Canberra has decided that it should have a seat at the table to help shape the global environment. In his bid launch, Albanese argued that foreign conflicts – and potential conflicts – will increasingly affect Australia’s security, economy, and way of life. A seat on the Security Council would give Australia a direct role in negotiating resolutions, responding to international crises, and shaping the U.N.’s approach to emerging security challenges. It would also provide an opportunity to strengthen Australia’s diplomatic relationships within and beyond the Indo-Pacific.
Central to Australia’s campaign is its commitment to an international order governed by rules rather than the exercise of power alone. As a middle power, Australia has a strong interest in protecting the sovereignty of smaller states and ensuring that international disputes are resolved through diplomacy rather than coercion. These principles have become pronounced following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and China’s disregard of UNCLOS in the South China Sea. Australia wants to use a Security Council seat to uphold international law, prevent conflict, and strengthen institutions that allow countries to determine their own futures without domination by larger powers.
This worldview may seem quaint. It is clear that three of the five permanent members of the Security Council – Russia, China, and the United States – have a lack of interest in upholding international law at present. A French presidential election in April 2027 may produce a new leader who likewise has a suspicion of the constraining power of international law. The ideals that Australia seeks to uphold may find little support among the Security Council’s most powerful members. 
Does this make Australia’s bid for a Security Council seat futile? 
It certainly makes what Australia would like to achieve more difficult. But there is now a certain pragmatism within Canberra, rather than an idealism or nostalgia for a previous era of geopolitics. The country will work with the global environment as it is to the advantage of Australia’s interests as best it can. 
The most practical response to this new era is to simply be in the rooms where the changes are taking place. Australia wants to be influential in how the world responds to emerging threats that extend beyond traditional military conflict. Cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and rapidly developing digital technologies are creating new vulnerabilities that require global responses. Many of the U.N. institutions were not designed to address such challenges, and Australia sees a role in helping shape how these institutions evolve. 
Alongside this, Australia’s ambition is also to be a voice for Pacific Island countries. A Security Council seat would provide another platform through which to advance the shared concerns of Pacific Islands Forum countries, particularly the relationship between climate change and international security. Australia has already identified ocean and climate security as priorities for its prospective term, recognizing that rising sea levels, environmental degradation, and resource insecurity present serious challenges to countries in its immediate region.
Yet the most important reason for gaining a Security Council seat will be to learn more about how the disruptive members of the Permanent Five think and bargain. For a country whose strategic environment is increasingly shaped by these disruptions, the best path to successful navigation is by knowing as much as possible about how the world is shifting through the interests, attitudes, and ideologies of the great powers.
When Australia last sat on the Security Council over a decade ago its role was simply to help reinforce an order that had broad support, and particularly the support of the United States. If Australia is successful in returning to the council in 2029 it will be under significantly different circumstances. Australia’s position now is that it cannot afford to be a bystander in this period of major geopolitical change. Restoring a world more comfortable to Australia seems unlikely, but making sure Australia can exert some influence as the rules are being rewritten is now vital.

articles.title: Why Is Brazil So Interested in ASEAN?
articles.full_text:
With its traditional markets less reliable, Brazil sees immense potential in Southeast Asia’s growing economies.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto shakes hands with Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva during talks in Planalto Palace, Brasília, Brazil, Jul. 9, 2025.
From September 7 to 10, Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira paid official visits to Singapore and Thailand. This followed his attendance at the 3rd Brazil-ASEAN Trilateral Meeting and the Conference of the High Contracting Parties to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia, held in Manila, from July 22 to 24. Between these two events, the secretary-general of ASEAN, Kao Kim Hourn, was invited by the Brazilian government to visit the country on a working visit from August 17 to 22. 
These events demonstrate the Brazilian government’s recent efforts to strengthen relations with ASEAN. It is worth remembering that, in 2025, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, made official visits to Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and attended the ASEAN Summit and East Asia Forum. Clearly, Brazil has clearly developed a strong interest in ASEAN and Southeast Asia, but why?
It is possible to say that one of the main reasons for such mobilization is the search for new markets. Since 2023, the Brazilian government has partnered with the private sector to expand its international client portfolio. According to the Ministry of Agriculture of Brazil, more than 500 new markets in 80 different countries opened for Brazilian agribusiness and fishing products. This is part of the new policy approach developed under Lula’s third term, with active participation of the Brazilian Trade and Investment Promotion Agency (Apex Brasil).
This strategy is especially important, as Brazil has come to the conclusion that the international scenario is now less predictable and increasingly protectionist than before, believing that is likely to remain so for an indefinite period of time. Indeed, Brazil is already facing challenges regarding the present and future of its economy.
In July 2026, the United States imposed additional tariffs of 25 percent and 12.5 percent on Brazilian products. The 25 percent tariff was related to an investigation by the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) under Section 301 into alleged disadvantages to the U.S. market. Similarly, the 12.5 percent tariff was introduced in response to USTR investigations under Section 301 concerning forced labor. These measures affected over 4,000 items exported by Brazil to the United States, collectively worth some $14.9 billion. 
Relations between the two countries have deteriorated as U.S. President Donald Trump holds right-wing views and has good relations with the Bolsonaro family, one of the most influential clans among Brazilian right-wing politicians and a political adversary of Lula and the left-wing Workers’ Party. Brazil’s federal government has stated that these tariffs are “not based on real facts” and are an attempt by the White House to influence Brazil’s domestic affairs and exert pressure on strategic assets such as rare earth reserves. Meanwhile, although interactions between the two leaders remain cordial, there is no truce or solution in sight.
Moreover, in May 2026, the European Commission announced restrictions on the import of animal meat products from Brazil based on EU Regulation 2019/6, concerning antimicrobial usage and cattle growth procedures. This decision was made shortly after the EU-Mercosur agreement came into force on May 1. The Brazilian government viewed the measure as a consequence of internal politics between European countries and their agricultural business groups. The latter had opposed the new agreement between the two trading blocs over concerns about the expected entry of South American agricultural products onto the market. The new restrictions came into force on September 3.  
In the long term, however, Brazil is also concerned about China’s intention to increase its food security and reduce its dependence on external partners. Food security became a major priority in China’s 15th Five-Year Plan, with measures established to increase domestic grain and meat production with the support of advanced technology. By 2025, Brazil’s exports to the Chinese market had reached $99.9 billion, accounting for 28.7 percent of all Brazilian exports. Of this total, $34.5 billion corresponded to soybeans and $9.7 billion to meat (red meat, pork, and poultry). If not addressed properly, an abrupt reduction in Chinese imports as China increases its self-sufficiency could pose a significant challenge to one of Brazil’s most important industries.
This scenario has increased the perception of Southeast Asia as a region of new opportunities for Brazilian companies. Information provided by Brazil’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs shows that trade between Brazil and ASEAN accounted for $38.4 billion in 2025, making the bloc Brazil’s fifth-largest trade partner, behind only China, the EU, the United States, and Mercosur. Furthermore, Brazil had a trade surplus of $10.3 billion with ASEAN during this period. 
Vieira, Brazil’s foreign minister, stated that trade with ASEAN will eventually surpass that with the U.S. and EU in the “near future.” This would make the ASEAN bloc Brazil’s second-largest trade partner. This outlook is supported by concrete evidence. According to Brazil’s MFA, Brazilian trade with ASEAN has increased by around 15 percent a year since 2020, which is significantly higher than with traditional trade partners. 
Indeed, trade has played a significant role in Lula’s visits to ASEAN countries. On each of his trips to the region, a business delegation accompanied the Brazilian president. Most of these delegates were from the agribusiness, food, defense, and aviation industries.
However, the rapprochement between Brazil and Southeast Asia was not only a consequence of commercial adversities; it was also a foreign policy strategy adopted by Brazil in order to strengthen diplomatic relations and trade ties. This was evident starting from Vieira’s trip to Indonesia, Cambodia, and the Philippines in 2023. 
Therefore, the recent sanctions and restrictions on Brazilian products cannot be viewed as the only cause of Brasilia’s interest in ASEAN, although these developments have incentivized greater commercial diversification. 
Brazil’s agriculture and food sectors see Southeast Asia as an opportunity to reach new markets and expand their client portfolio due to the region’s large population and growing purchasing power, which could boost the demand for food products, especially more expensive ones such as meat. 
For example, JBS, a Brazilian multinational and the world’s largest meat processing company, recognizes OECD and FAO forecasts that global meat consumption will increase until 2034, led by countries such as Indonesia, the Philippines, and Vietnam. JBS was present during official visits to the region and has already announced investments and secured deals in Southeast Asia. 
In March 2025, shortly after Vietnam announced that it would open up to Brazilian meat products, JBS announced a direct investment worth $100 million. These funds will be used to construct two meat processing plants in Vietnam for the production of imported Brazilian red meat, pork, and poultry.
Moreover, in August 2026, JBS formed a strategic partnership with Dantara Investment Management (DIM), the Indonesian sovereign wealth fund and investment agency. The partnership aims to establish a joint venture that will expand JBS’s business in the protein market in Indonesia, as well as in Southeast Asia, Australia, and New Zealand. JBS will transfer its Australian and New Zealand operations to the new subsidiary, which will form the basis of the joint venture, while DIM will invest $2.5 billion initially to acquire a 25 percent stake in the new partnership. 
It is possible that other Brazilian food companies will follow JBS’s lead and expand into Asian markets as potential investments are disclosed and profits start to be announced.
But Brazil’s economic interest isn’t limited to the food sector. Since 2023, Brazilian aerospace corporation Embraer has been attempting to access the aviation market in Southeast Asia in order to expand its portfolio, which is currently focused on companies in the U.S. and Europe. According to Embraer’s Market Outlook, published in July 2026, the global market will require around 8,500 commercial aircraft with a capacity of 150 passengers by 2045, 1,050 of which will be delivered to the Asia-Pacific region. 
To capture some of these orders, Embraer is promoting its E-Jets E2 line, which is designed for regional flights. Currently, only Scoot, a Singaporean airline, operates E-Jets in Southeast Asia, with nine E190-E2 aircraft leased from the U.S. company Azorra. In 2023, Embraer closed a deal with Malaysian airline SKS Airways for ten E195-E2 aircraft, but this was subsequently cancelled due to SKS’s financial difficulties, resulting in the airline ceasing operations in the country.
Since then, Embraer has been trying to find new Southeast Asian airlines to operate its jets. During Lula’s official visits, Embraer executives attended meetings with high-ranking officials to promote E-Jets as a solution for regional air connectivity. They also highlighted the possibility of establishing service and maintenance repair centers, offering direct investment opportunities in the chosen country, knowledge-sharing, and contracts with local manufacturers for supplying aircraft parts. A maintenance center in Southeast Asia would give Embraer a competitive advantage, making E-Jets more appealing to regional airlines. No formal agreements have yet been signed regarding the acquisition of E-jets or the establishment of a maintenance center.
The examples from JBS and Embraer are particularly notable, as they demonstrate that Brazilian companies are willing not only to export to Southeast Asia, but also to adapt their international strategies to the region. JBS’s new processing plants in Vietnam and its joint venture with DIM, for example, provide access to a growing market and strengthen its presence through intra-regional operations and production. The same applies to Embraer’s proposal for a maintenance and repair center, which would connect regional production to the company’s supply chain network. While the investment method does not prevent vulnerabilities to geopolitical or regulatory adversities, it can contribute to the diversification of trade relations and the creation of new growth opportunities.
From the Southeast Asian perspective, the conflict in the Gulf region has sparked concerns that over-reliance on a few suppliers would create dependence and compromise reliable energy supplies. Consequently, these countries have been searching for new suppliers, with Petrobras emerging as one of the available options. Since the war between the United States and Iran began, Brazil’s state-controlled oil company has increased its oil production, reaching 3.34 million barrels per day (bpd) in the second quarter. This figure represents a 14.1 percent increase compared to the same period in 2025 and a 3.4 percent increase compared to the first quarter of 2026. This was mainly driven by developments in Pre-Salt operations and the commissioning of new platforms. 
Petrobras has since increased exports to Southeast Asia. From January to June, traditional clients such as Singapore and Indonesia increased their imports of Brazilian oil by 28 percent and 157 percent, respectively. New clients have also emerged, including the Philippines and Myanmar. From January to August 2026, Brazil exported the equivalent of $4.6 billion worth of crude oil and fuel oil to Southeast Asia.
It’s true that Brazil is concerned about the situation with its primary trade partners, and the shift toward ASEAN is an effective alternative for dealing with increasing sanctions and restrictions. However, Brazil’s interest in Southeast Asia is not merely a reaction to the current situation. The government’s strategy has included trade diversification since 2023, aiming to deal with a volatile, and increasingly protectionist, international environment. 
This scenario provides an opportunity for ASEAN-Brazil relations, as Southeast Asian countries are also eager to reach new trade partners, attract investment, and connect with global supply chains. The cases of JBS, Embraer, and Petrobras exemplify this scenario and the opportunities arising from it, which allow Brazil and Southeast Asia to deepen relations beyond governmental diplomacy. Businesses are already identifying concrete opportunities in the region, while the increasing diplomatic dialogue helps to consolidate this connection. 
This suggests that Southeast Asia could become a relevant component of a broader trade diversification strategy of Brazil. If Lula wins the October elections and secures a fourth term, Brazil is expected to continue its shift toward the East and possibly explore not only trade partnerships, but also deeper bilateral and multilateral partnerships with ASEAN countries. In many respects, ASEAN-Brazil relations remain at an early stage.
From September 7 to 10, Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira paid official visits to Singapore and Thailand. This followed his attendance at the 3rd Brazil-ASEAN Trilateral Meeting and the Conference of the High Contracting Parties to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia, held in Manila, from July 22 to 24. Between these two events, the secretary-general of ASEAN, Kao Kim Hourn, was invited by the Brazilian government to visit the country on a working visit from August 17 to 22.
articles.summary: With its traditional markets less reliable, Brazil sees immense potential in Southeast Asia's growing economies.

articles.title: What Will Indonesia Do With Its New Aircraft Carrier?
articles.full_text:
The KRI Sriwijaya is a small aircraft carrier and may be better understood as an amphibious support ship.
Febry Triantama has asked difficult questions in these pages about the strategic reasoning behind Indonesia’s acquisition of KRI Sriwijaya, a small aircraft carrier formerly owned and operated as the Giuseppe Garibaldi by the Italian Navy. Much regarding the future of the carrier (and the future of the Indonesian Navy) depends on how much Indonesia invests in maintaining and optimizing the vessel and its air wing.
The acquisition of the warship puts Indonesia into a growing club of navies in the Western Pacific to operate aircraft carriers. In recent years Australia, India, China, and Japan have all built or acquired flat-decked aircraft carrying warships. Most of these are considerably larger than the new Indonesian warship and can accordingly carry more and more varied aircraft and operate at greater distances from base. Thailand joined the aircraft carrier club in the 1990s with the Spanish-designed Chakri Naruebet, similar in size to KRI Sriwijaya. 
Two decades ago vessels like the Thai and Indonesian carriers might be expected to operate V/STOL (vertical or short take off and landing) fighters. But it does not appear that Indonesia will go this route. The world’s only operational V/STOL fighters are the AV-8B Harrier and the F-35B Lightning II; the former are old and expensive to operate, while the latter have yet to be offered to Jakarta, and in any case are extremely expensive. The Sriwijaya is better understood as an amphibious support ship than as an aircraft carrier, a warship with substantial aviation capabilities but without an airwing capable of offensive or defense air superiority operations. This would place the ship in the same category as Australia’s Canberra-class landing helicopter docks (LHDs). 
The best model for the Indonesia Navy may be the TCG Anadolu, a Turkish amphibious warship built along the same lines as vessels operating for Spain and Australia. While Anadolu was originally expected to fly the F-35B, disputes with Washington have put those plans on ice, perhaps permanently. Instead, the Turkish Navy has used Anadolu as a platform for experimenting with a variety of uncrewed aircraft, including the Bayraktar TB3 and the Bayraktar Kimilelma, both of which have multimission capabilities. Following the Turkish lead would allow Indonesia to avoid the expense of acquiring F-35Bs and, perhaps more importantly, the difficulties of maintaining trained pilots and aircrew for a very small combat wing. Indonesia has already signed a deal with Turkiye for the transfer of a number of drones, and may be able to take advantage of Turkiye’s experience operating advanced UAVs from a maritime platform. 
If Anadolu represents the best case, the Thai Chakri Naruebet represents the worst. The Thai carrier was initially expected to operate AV-8B Harriers, but the notoriously difficult fighter proved too much of a hassle and the small force was retired in the early 2000s. Since the Chakri Naruebet has become known as a “harbor queen,” barely operational beyond a few high profile humanitarian assistance/disaster relief (HADR) operations. Thailand had expected more from its carrier but serial financial crises de-emphasized the navy and the navy’s most expensive ship. 
Of course, Indonesia is considerably larger than Thailand and its navy has far greater responsibilities. The Sriwijaya is an older vessel and will require considerable modification before service, but Indonesia has already engaged with Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri to modernize the warship, an arrangement that should also improve Indonesia’s capacity for keeping the ship at sea. 
An aircraft carrier of any size is a huge opportunity, but also a huge responsibility. Indonesia is rolling the dice on its capacity to keep the ship in service, as well as on the durability of a very old vessel. It could pay off with a much enhanced HADR capability, as well as a platform capable of taking advantage of the latest in drone technology. Or Indonesia could end up with its own harbor queen.

articles.title: Goodbye, ‘China Plus One’: The Real Change in US China Policy
articles.full_text:
Beneath the pageantry, here’s the change that matters: Washington has stopped talking about leaving China.
U.S. President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping of China arrive via the Cross Hall to a State Arrival ceremony on the State Floor of the White House, Sep.24, 2026.
U.S. President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet for President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington and greeted him in person at Joint Base Andrews on the evening of September 23, a rare gesture for an American president. Critics in both parties warned that the pageantry would reward a rival. 
However, the red carpet, the state dinner with its exquisite menu, the cannon salute and the bald eagle sculpture gifted to Xi are just the surface. Beneath them, the bilateral relationship has begun to take a new direction. 
At their Beijing summit in May, the two leaders agreed to build a “constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability.” It’s a lengthy phrase, but each word is there for a reason. “Constructive” commits both sides to a positive agenda, not just damage control. “Strategic” places the relationship at the level of leaders and long horizons. “Stability” sets a direction and boundary for the relationship. 
This new formula is sharply different from the language used to describe China-U.S. relations since 2018.
Recall Trump’s first term. Washington launched a trade war, imposed tariffs on Chinese goods, and placed Huawei and other Chinese firms under technology sanctions. Washington urged multinational companies to quickly adopt “China Plus One” strategies, moving out of China and building a second supply base in Vietnam, India, or Mexico. It trumpeted decoupling as the goal. 
Since 2018, Beijing has gradually diversified its trade across Southeast Asia, Latin America, and Africa. China-U.S. trade fell by around 30 percent in 2025 alone, according to the McKinsey Global Institute’s 2026 update on the geometry of global trade. Meanwhile, China built a complete and strategically critical supply chain, from basic materials to advanced equipment. China now is the only country to make goods in all 41 industrial categories and 666 sub-categories in the United Nations classification. 
Today, China sells advanced machinery, components and critical materials to other countries’ factories. McKinsey called it the factory to the world factories, and the Wall Street Journal described the same shift. In many ways, China Plus One did not remove China from the global supply chain. Instead, it has helped China move up the value chain, as India, Vietnam, and Mexico become assembly lines for Chinese products.
These economic shifts have resulted in a telling change in Washington’s vocabulary. In August 2023, then-U.S. Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo said that China was “uninvestable.” This became the preferred talking point of politicians and China hawks across Washington. For years, terms like “de-risking,” “de-coupling,” “friend-shoring” and “China+ Plus One” filled congressional hearings, cable interviews, and opinion pages. 
However, references to China Plus One have nearly vanished in Washington. No one among the Trump administration’s senior officials and business executives uses the term anymore. 
The change was also symbolized by the guests at the head table during the state dinner for Xi. Beside the two presidents were Tim Cook of Apple, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX. All of them understand how critical China is to their businesses, both as a market and as the base of their supply chains. 
Apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, was developed, trial-produced and assembled exclusively in China, according to Apple’s vice president for Asia procurement and operations, not built in India or Vietnam. Tesla previously announced plants to phase Chinese suppliers out of its American-built cars. Now it is seeking multiple suppliers in China for its Optimus humanoid robot, and orders have already been placed. Huang has argued for months that export controls are backfiring on American competitiveness. Su has pledged to deepen AMD’s engagement in China. These executives know China Plus One and decoupling with China are not working. 
Smaller firms follow the same logic. EnerVenue, a California battery startup, announced last week that it began mass production in Changzhou after abandoning plans for a $264 million factory in Kentucky. Its chief executive cited China’s skilled workforce and supply chain strength, and called China the “factory of factories.” Chinese business media have also reported cases of American manufacturers that moved orders to India or Southeast Asia to avoid tariffs, struggled with quality and delivery, and returned the work to their original Chinese suppliers. 
The toasts at the state dinner on September 24 affirmed the new direction, especially in the people-to-people and business-to-business ties. Both leaders reached back into history. Trump spoke of the foundation of commerce and mutual respect, and of ties between the two peoples that endure. 
Xi recalled the trade that began soon after American independence and the Hump airlift over the Himalayas during the war against Japan. He recalled “ping-pong diplomacy,” and the redwoods Richard Nixon gave China that now grow in Zhejiang. He praised Ronald Sakolsky, an American teacher who donated $5,000 to fund a Chinese woman’s desert tree-planting two decades ago and recently returned to China to see a forest in the desert.
Xi’s most strategic move was his remark that Trump’s Make America Great Again and China’s pursuit of national rejuvenation “can surely be mutually reinforcing.” This is a strategic discourse specifically aimed at the idea that dominates Washington’s thinking about the China-U.S. relationship: the Thucydides Trap, which holds that a rising power and an established one are headed for war. Xi’s remark rejected that premise and offered an alternative frame. Two great projects of national renewal need not collide. He called for “a new approach for major countries to get along.”
None of this means rivalry and competition between the two great powers have slowed down. In July the Federal Communications Commission added foreign-made humanoid and industrial robots to its covered list, a move Beijing condemned. Chip export controls remain unchanged. China’s rare earth magnet shipments to the United States fell 21 percent in August to 512 tons, heading toward their lowest level since 2021. Taiwan, Iran, and AI safety will test the newly coined “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” But both leaders have endorsed its guardrails.
While Trump 1.0 started decoupling and China Plus One, Trump 2.0 now regards China as an equal partner in deals, a critical supplier the American economy cannot easily replace, and the other half of a G2. 
The festivities at Joint Base Andrews and in the East Room of the White House will soon fade from the headlines. But Washington has stopped talking about leaving China, and corporate America never really left.

articles.title: India’s Javelin Deal: The Unending Loop of Procurement
articles.full_text:
The deal is one of the earliest defense deals between India and the U.S. It is also the one that dragged on the longest.
“BIG news! India plans to buy the battle-tested Javelin anti-tank system,” U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor announced on X on August 28, as the Indian Army signed the letter of offer and acceptance (LOA) for the purchase of the missile system through the foreign military sales (FMS) route, also adding that it’s opening the door to “co-production possibilities.” For the Indian Army, it marks 16 years of ups and downs and the long lead time to fill a critical capability gap in anti-tank guided missiles (ATGM), even if only piecemeal.
The Javelin is a versatile, one-man-portable and platform-mounted fire-and-forget anti-tank precision weapon system that is capable of defeating all kinds of armor and fortified positions. It is in service with more than 25 countries, including the U.S. Army and the U.S. Marine Corps.
Following this, Lockheed announced a memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Tata Advanced Systems Limited (TASL) and the Javelin Joint Venture (JJV), a partnership between Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, for the “co-production of the Javelin All Up Round (AUR) in India.” The MoU will explore establishing a final assembly and integration facility for the Javelin AUR, along with component production capabilities, in India, Lockheed said in a statement.
While the specifics of the LOA haven’t been released yet, the U.S. Defense Security Cooperation Agency notification of November 2025 said that India would purchase 100 Javelin rounds and 25 launch units at an estimated cost of $45.7 million.
The entire saga can be viewed through two prisms: the deepening India-U.S. defense cooperation, and India’s rickety military modernization epitomized by the Javelin saga.
The nearly 1.3 million-strong Indian Army started looking for a new generation fire-and-forget ATGM in the early 2000s to replace the Konkurs and Milan in service. The overall requirement is for over 40,000 missiles to equip the 382 infantry battalions and 44 mechanized regiments. However, as the indigenous effort by the Defense Research and Development Organization (DRDO) was delayed, the Army started looking for import options to partly fill the deficiency.
In August 2010, Defense Minister A. K. Antony informed the Indian parliament that his ministry proposed to issue a letter of request to the U.S. government for procurement of the Javelin ATGM along with transfer of technology under their FMS route. After the issue of the letter of request, further procurement-related necessary action will follow, he added.
The Army’s first experience with the Javelin came in 2009 during the bilateral exercise Yudh Abhyas, where the U.S. Army fielded it and so, was under consideration. While it was extensively tested, the deal didn’t move forward due to U.S. technology transfer limitations. This was when the Army moved to acquire the Spike ATGM manufactured by Rafael Advanced Defense Systems of Israel.
The Defense Acquisition Council, the highest decision-making body on procurements in the Ministry of Defense, accorded initial approval for procurement of Spike in 2009 for over 8,000 missiles and 300 launchers with technology transfer for their domestic manufacture, a deal worth $500 million. It was approved in October 2014, but the contract negotiations went into a loop over cost and technology transfer.
In fact, in 2016, in anticipation of the deal and to meet the domestic manufacturing requirement, Rafael set up a joint venture with Kalyani Group to manufacture sub-assemblies, with defense public sector firm Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) being the system integrator. The deal was cancelled in January 2018, just ahead of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to India visit, as it was felt that indigenous development was making progress. However, the deal was revived soon after, by the end of 2018, for the purchase of 170 launchers, 4,500 missiles and 15 simulators. This too dragged on for a few years but never came to fruition due to questions being raised over the missile’s performance during the validation trials.
All through this, the Javelin was never fully out of the picture.
After the Balakot air strike in February 2019 in response to the Pulwama terrorist attack and simmering tensions with Pakistan, the Army procured a small number of Spike-LR (long-range) ATGMs under the emergency procurement route sanctioned by the MoD to fill critical deficiencies. The order was for 12 launchers and around 250 missiles. The Army repeated the order for the Spike-LR in 2020 in another round of Emergency Procurement sanctioned after the standoff with China along the disputed border at Ladakh.
Orders were capped at 3 billion Indian rupees, valued at $42 million in 2019. The Spike-LR, a 4th-gen missile with a range of up to 4 kilometers, is a different variant from the one originally tested. This remains the only new generation ATGM inducted by the Indian Army in the whole period.
Given the long and convoluted procurement process, emergency procurement has become the preferred way to fast-track critical procurements.
India-U.S. Defense Industrial Cooperation
The Javelin deal, which emerged out of growing India-U.S. bilateral defense and strategic cooperation, is one of the earliest defense deals between the two countries and the one that dragged on the longest.
Incidentally, the Javelin was also tested in 2024 along with Stryker infantry combat vehicles. However, the performance of the missile was sub-optimal as the lot provided for trials was dated. While the Stryker deal drags on, Operation Sindoor in 2025 reinforced the deficiencies.
The Javelin deal strengthens the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership and also opens discussions on mutually beneficial co-production and additional opportunities to strengthen the defense industrial bases of both countries, a U.S. Embassy statement said. The local manufacture of assemblies and parts of the Javelin fits into the overall deepening of India’s presence in the supply chains of U.S. companies manufacturing components and sub-assemblies.
TASL itself is now a major player in this segment with a series of tie-ups with U.S. defense majors. For instance, with Boeing, it manufactures fuselages, secondary structures and vertical spar boxes for AH-64 Apache attack helicopters, and vertical fins for 737 aircraft; and fixed wings for Lockheed Martin’s C-130J and F-16 aircraft. Such integration of Indian industry over the last two decades has positioned the U.S. as India’s top defense export destination.
While India has significantly increased its defense procurements from the U.S., the effort for co-development and co-production has had no real success to date. The crown jewel of that effort, the license manufacture of the GE-414 jet engine domestically to power the Light Combat Aircraft-Mk2, has been stuck for several years now.
Though small as a system, the Javelin is high in its battlefield impact and will be a step forward in the joint endeavor. That this was announced amid the current turbulence in the India-U.S. relationship showcases the distance travelled by the two countries on the defense and strategic front.
Acquisition of the Javelin too is through the Emergency Procurement route that limits the numbers that can be purchased. The larger requirement of the Indian Army for ATGMs remains unfulfilled.
An ATGM is a critical battlefield weapon whose importance has grown manifold since its utility was underscored in Ukraine and other conflicts. While the Indian armed forces look at niche and emerging technologies, procurement of several other such basic but critical systems are caught in a loop. This merits immediate attention and action even as India keeps Operation Sindoor rolling and prepares for the next round of confrontation with Pakistan.
While development of the indigenous man-portable ATGM by DRDO has made progress, the timelines are still long. Coupled with evolving threats, this Javelin deal is likely the first of many.

Following this, Lockheed announced a memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Tata Advanced Systems Limited (TASL) and the Javelin Joint Venture (JJV), a partnership between Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, for the “co-production of the Javelin All Up Round (AUR) in India.” The MoU will explore establishing a final assembly and integration facility for the Javelin AUR, along with component production capabilities, in India, Lockheed said in a statement.
While the specifics of the LOA haven’t been released yet, the U.S. Defense Security Cooperation Agency notification of November 2025 said that India would purchase 100 Javelin rounds and 25 launch units at an estimated cost of $45.7 million.
The entire saga can be viewed through two prisms: the deepening India-U.S. defense cooperation, and India’s rickety military modernization epitomized by the Javelin saga.
articles.summary: The deal is one of the earliest defense deals between India and the U.S. It is also the one that dragged on the longest.

articles.title: The Future of Shipbuilding in Southeast Asia
articles.full_text:
There are significant opportunities – and risks.
Global shipbuilding demand is likely to remain resilient for the long-term, with increasing geopolitical conflict and uncertainty one of the primary drivers. The 2026 war between Iran, the United States and Israel has caused a spike in demand for alternative suppliers and routes, leading Fitch Rating to revise sectoral outlook to “neutral” from “deteriorating.” According to the non-profit Container Trades Statistics, global container volumes reached 16.2 million 20-foot-equivalent units (mTEUs) in April — the first full month of data since the Strait of Hormuz closures triggered by February’s Persian Gulf crisis — marking a 4 percent year-over-year increase and a 1.6 percent rise over March. Year-to-date volumes are also running 5 percent ahead of 2025 levels.
Shipping sector analysts also predicted that the market had become oversaturated with vessel capacity and fewer orders would be placed to shipbuilders in 2026 and 2027. However, geopolitical disruptions are one major reason why orders have remained strong. Shocks such as Red Sea attacks, the Russia-Ukraine war, the Panama Canal drought, the Baltimore bridge collapse, and now the Iran-Israel-US conflict have demonstrated the importance of excess capacity. Carriers can more easily navigate these conflicts with a large and diverse fleet, resulting in expansive orderbooks that are now treated as insurance rather than oversupply.
These trends are good news to the world’s leading shipbuilding nations, which are highly concentrated in East Asia, particularly China. However, in the current geopolitical climate, there are significant opportunities for Southeast Asian nations to scale up their shipbuilding industries and take advantage of the sustained demand for global trade.
Southeast Asian nations are taking the initiative to capture greater shipbuilding market share through structured international partnerships. At the OECD-Southeast Asia Policy Roundtable on Shipbuilding, Steel, and AI held in Tokyo in February 2026, Indonesia, Vietnam, and Thailand agreed to a regional peer review of their shipbuilding sectors with the OECD, covering priorities such as workforce skills, technical capabilities, supply chain dependencies, energy-efficient ships, and leveling the competitive playing field. The Philippines separately agreed to follow up on implementation pathways for OECD peer review recommendations, while all four countries were invited to join the OECD’s shipbuilding committee meeting in Paris in April.

articles.title: Uzbekistan’s Death Penalty Debate Returns After Child Abuse Case
articles.full_text:
The debate over the death penalty is back in Uzbekistan, this time involving the country’s most senior officials.
For the second time in the  span of a year a brutal child abuse case has sparked heated public discussion in Uzbekistan. Reportedly, a five-year-old girl was repeatedly raped in a public kindergarten by a facilities manager who worked at the school in the Uchkurgan district of Namangan. According to the mother of the survivor, the alleged perpetrator is their neighbor and she became suspicious after she saw him smiling at her five-year-old daughter. She gently asked the girl questions only to find out that the facilities manager would buy sweets for the girl, tell her he loved her, and promised to buy more presents and sweets if she didn’t expose him. The mother suspects the man had threatened her daughter.  
Last year a similar case, which also occurred in Namangan, where a previously imprisoned convict raped a seven-year-old girl, caused a wave of demands by the public to restore the death penalty for serious crimes such as the sexual assault of minors. Public discussions over the death penalty typically emerge in Uzbekistan after news of an especially brutal crime against children breaks. An earlier wave of loud discussions took place in 2024 after a three-year-old was stabbed 12 times. 
What’s new this time is that high-ranking political figures are getting involved. 
Saida Mirziyoyeva, the head of the presidential administration and a deputy chair of the Security Council (and also the president’s daughter) chimed in. “In my opinion, the death penalty should be used for such heinous crimes. Unfortunately, the current legislation does not provide for the death penalty,” she wrote on her Telegram channel on September 27. 
“We are preparing a proposal to amend the legislation to maximize liability for this type of crime,” she added. 
Echoing Mirziyoyeva’s words, Alisher Qodirov, leader of the Milliy Tiklanish (National Revival) Democratic Party and deputy speaker of the Uzbek parliament, called death penalty a “necessity.” Qodirov is famous for making nationalist, sometimes controversial statements. 
“The continued existence of those who intentionally kill innocent people, especially child murderers and pedophiles, is a motivation for further crimes of this kind!” Qodirov wrote on his Telegram, reposting Mirziyoyeva’s earlier statement. 
This is not the first time Qodirov has voiced his position on the death penalty. Previously, in 2024, after news reports about a three-year-old girl being murdered, Qodirov suggested “cleansing” society. “It’s illogical to use our taxes to support a criminal who’s become an animal, keep him healthy, feed him, and then wait for someone else to die! Society needs to be cleansed of such people!” he wrote.
Both Mirziyoyeva and Qodirov know that Uzbekistan abolished capital punishment in 2008 and acceded to the Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR aimed at abolition. Uzbekistan has no mechanism to reinstate the death penalty without a much larger legal overhaul, and no such overhaul is presently underway.
In a rather unusual course of developments for Uzbekistan, the discussion over the death penalty divided the country’s political parties. As a new bill to increase liability for violence against children was introduced to the Legislative Chamber on September 29, Qodirov announced a neutral position on the proposed bill and doubled down on his stance regarding the need to resurrect the death penalty. Qodirov referred to Norwegian neo-Nazi and mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik, stating that he had complained “about the lack of facilities for writing a book, and those conditions were subsequently provided for him.” 
Qodirov’s interpretation isn’t quite accurate. While Breivik did complain about the “stab-resistant” pen he was made to write with and was reportedly provided with an electronic typewriter, Breivik’s communications continue to be censored by prison authorities and he has not published a book.
Nevertheless, using Breivik as a point of reference, Qodirov questioned the compatibility of Uzbek values and international law. 
“Whose footsteps are we following!?” he asked. “We will also be forced to create conditions for our pedophile if he asks, because the international law we follow sees him as a human being, not as a dead person.”
Bobur Bekmurodov, a member of the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis and leader of the Yuksalish movement, opposed Qodirov’s statements openly. His arguments are clear: the constitution prohibits the death penalty, bringing the death penalty back could put child victims in greater danger, break Uzbekistan’s international obligations and raise the possibility of errors in judicial practices. 
“If child rape is punishable by death, there is nothing to stop the perpetrator from destroying the only witness, the child himself,” wrote Bekmurodov.
While the grief over the case is genuine, the debate over the death penalty is a populist, opportunistic response. In a country where no other important questions are debated by high (or  low) profile politicians, children and women’s abuse is a risk-free topic. Not only does it attract empathy from millions of citizens, but it also gains praise from international organizations. Siding with an innocent child is always a winning move. 
As outrage grows, officials do their best to appease the public. The investigation over the case is now under the prosecutor general’s control. Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva, another daughter of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and the first deputy director of the National Agency for Social Protection, reported that her agency is also involved in the case and the survivor’s family will be moved to another city and provided with housing. The agency also suggested changing the girl’s surname to ensure her privacy as she rehabilitates. The Ministry of Preschool and School Education formed a working group to address the situation.
Right now, all attention is being given to maximizing punishment for one perpetrator and not letting another incident happen. What is left out of these debates is the failure of the systems that should have protected this girl. The mother of the survivor told local media that the cameras in the kindergarten did not record anything that day. And more absurdly, she had been told that the perpetrator was responsible for the cameras. The perpetrator’s wife allegedly offered her a bribe to close the case, too. 
The staff of the kindergarten  who are supposed to protect the children in their care, are hiding behind paperwork instead of showing compassion. The director of the kindergarten said she was on a holiday when the alleged incident occurred and she had already provided explanatory letters to the police. She also added that children are never left unsupervised. The girl’s teacher also swore the girl was never left alone – “Not an hour, not a minute, would [she] be left unattended.”
Local media outlets and the authorities have not disclosed the perpetrator’s name or released a mugshot. Netizens, however, have found his photos and full name and doxed his identity on social media pages. 
Yesterday, Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva noted that her agency, together with other relevant bodies, had been working on a draft law that would introduce life imprisonment for crimes involving child sexual abuse.
“We also propose to strengthen the responsibility of parents for neglecting children and of educators for allowing violence and discrimination, and to provide legal assistance and protection to child victims at every stage of the investigation and trial,” the agency’s Telegram post stated.
From 2022 to 2026 445 cases of rape involving minors under 14 years old were formally registered in Uzbekistan. Not all cases make headlines. Journalist and economist Bakhodir Abdullayev noted that the legislation on lifetime imprisonment for sexual abuse of minors was supposed to be passed by April 2026. But it wasn’t until the current furor, when it became politically expedient to take action, that the legislature actually moved.
The Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis passed the bill on September 29.
