articles.title: The Trump-Xi Summit Is Over, But Taiwan Is Still Bracing for the Fallout
articles.full_text:
Given what happened in May, Taiwanese may have been more nervous after the latest Trump-Xi summit ended.
U.S. President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping of China arrive via the Cross Hall to a State Arrival ceremony on the State Floor of the White House, Sep.24, 2026.
The latest meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping led to much anxiety in Taiwan, with fears that Trump could potentially throw Taiwan under the bus in the course of negotiations with Xi. The two leaders agreed to dialogue on AI, as well as tariff reductions on $30 billion in “non-sensitive goods” going both ways. Even so, readouts between the two sides differed as to what was agreed to be purchased, and any discussion of semiconductors, chips, and export controls was not mentioned. 
Besides trade deals, there have been few concrete outcomes from the meeting to date, and the two leaders initially remained silent when asked by reporters if Taiwan featured in their summit. Trump later denied that Taiwan was discussed at length, then stated that he and Xi “didn’t spend a lot of time talking about Taiwan.”
Other reports suggest that Xi tried press Trump to curtail support for Taiwan, and accept Beijing’s framing on Taiwan. Chinese state-run media quoted Xi as stating during the meeting: “I hope that the United States adheres to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’ and handles the Taiwan issue prudently.” 
In particular, ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting, international media reporting suggested that Xi would try to convince Trump to cut weapons sales to Taiwan. Although the Trump administration approved $11 billion in arms sales to Taiwan last December, the Trump administration has yet to approve a further $14 billion package. 
It was generally understood that Trump would not approve the arms sale ahead of his meeting with Xi, in order to ensure that the talks went smoothly. For its part, the Taiwanese government has attempted to reassure the public that ties with the United States are stable, and reiterated that U.S. policy on Taiwan has not changed after the summit. Nevertheless, the real question will be whether Trump reveals any unexpected curveballs for Taiwan after the meeting itself. 
If so, this would follow the precedent set by Trump after his meeting with Xi in May 2026 in Beijing. Little happened during the meeting itself, which was mostly a non-event. In May, as with this latest summit, Trump initially declined to answer questions on Taiwan from reporters. The readouts of the May 2026 meeting differed between the United States and China, with the U.S. denying that Taiwan had come up at all, while China claimed that it had been discussed. As if to forestall a potential shift in position by Trump,  U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio emphasized during the May trip that U.S. policy on Taiwan was unchanged in an interview with NBC. 
During an interview with Fox News shortly after his return from China, however, Trump seemed to hit out at Taiwan, stating that he was “not looking to have somebody go independent,” and that Taiwan needed “cool down a bit.” Trump then moved on to attack Taiwan with accusations that it had stolen the U.S. semiconductor industry, while calling on semiconductor companies to move back to the United States. 
Most alarming of all, Trump cast doubt on U.S. commitment to Taiwan as a whole, while suggesting that the Taiwan-U.S. relationship was mostly transactional. In particular, Trump suggested that arms sales to Taiwan were up for negotiation, and that this made for a “good bargaining chip” in talks with China. 
Such comments provoked alarm in Taiwan, seeing as this contravenes U.S. commitments to provide weapons to Taiwan dating back to the Reagan-era Three Assurances. Trump also raised questions about whether the United States would intervene in the event of a conflict with China, stating that he did not think it was logical for American troops to “travel 9,500 miles to fight a war.”
Given that recent history, Taiwanese may have been more nervous after the latest Trump-Xi summit ended. 
Indeed, indications have since emerged that Trump offered to sell arms to China during his September meeting with Xi. David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, stated that Trump made such comments to Xi in an interview with Fox News on September 27. Although Perdue also stated that U.S. policy remained unchanged on Taiwan, this was an unusual comment by Trump. The offer came only a few days after controversy erupted about F-35 parts that were mistakenly diverted to Hong Kong, raising concerns about sensitive U.S. military technology ending up in Chinese hands. 
As such, while Taiwan may have breathed a sigh of relief that the September summit has not resulted in any overt shift in U.S. policy on Taiwan, what remains is to see whether Trump shifts later on. As some analysts have noted, Trump has already echoed Chinese language on Taiwan on numerous occasions in the past. And while some elements of his administration, such as Rubio, may emphasize that policy remains unchanged, this is not reassuring when Trump himself contradicts those statements.
It is still uncertain when further U.S. arms sales to Taiwan will be approved. Trump and Xi are set to meet two more times this year, in November at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, as well as at the G20 summit in December at the Trump National Doral Miami Golf Club in Florida. It is possible that Trump will hold off on arms sales until after these meetings, or until 2027. Trump’s decision whether to approve arms sales or not could also be impacted by the U.S. midterm elections in November. 
With the Trump administration holding off on approving arms sales to Taiwan, this may complicate the domestic debate on defense spending. In past years, the United States has sought to pressure Taiwan to increase defense spending to 5 percent or even 10 percent of GDP, with Trump himself suggesting that the U.S. should not defend Taiwan if Taiwan is not serious about its own defense. 
But at a time of stark partisanship, the Kuomintang (KMT) delayed for over 200 days on reviewing the central government budget, while enacting widespread cuts to government ministries it views as antagonistic. The delays impacted defense spending, as well as spending on Taiwan’s domestic drone program. Even so, the KMT suddenly reversed course in August to finally approve the budget, though it limited drone spending by passing it as part of the central government budget rather than as a special expenditure. 
Efforts by the United States to push Taiwan to increase defense spending are likely to ring hollow in Taiwan if Washington refuses to sell Taiwan arms. Likewise, comments by Trump will increase doubts about U.S. reliability as an ally in wartime – indeed, survey polling shows that skepticism about the U.S. is up across the board in Taiwan. (Such polling also shows an increase in the Taiwanese public’s willingness to fight – even without U.S. intervention.) Certainly, with the United States holding off on arms sales to Taiwan for so long, Trump suddenly offering to sell arms to China is not likely to reaffirm faith in the U.S. in Taiwan. 
Increased skepticism about U.S. reliability is likely to lead to efforts to shore up Taiwan’s domestic defense programs, which are not reliant on the mercurial nature of arms sales. Taiwan is especially likely to seek cooperation from non-U.S. partners on drone development, while positioning itself as an alternative to drone supply chains highly reliant on China. 
It can be expected that summits between Trump and Xi will fall into this familiar script going forward – even when the meetings themselves may result in little substance, the point is to see what occurs afterward, and how left-field comments or actions by Trump are perceived.

articles.title: Ismat Ara on India’s Crackdown on Love
articles.full_text:
Ara explains the insidious harm of the “love jihad” myth: “A deeply personal decision, two people deciding to marry, gradually becomes something that others felt entitled to violently police.”
Love and marriage across religious and caste lines have always been frowned upon and forbidden in India. However, Hindu right-wing organizations have taken this to a new extreme by conjuring up a conspiracy theory they term “love jihad.” India is witnessing a systematic strategy being implemented by Hindutva activists to not just prevent Hindu women from marrying Muslim men but to malign the latter by ascribing to them sinister motives of enticing Hindu women with false promises of love and marriage for the sole purpose of converting them to Islam. Bharatiya Janata Party politicians have used the “love jihad” bogey to deepen Hindu anxieties and polarize society. BJP governments in several states have enacted anti-religious conversion laws. Meanwhile, right-wing goons have wreaked enormous havoc in the lives of young couples who dare to love across religious lines.
In her recent book, “Under a Saffron Sky: Inside India’s Crackdown on Love,” author Ismat Ara recounts the enormous stress and suffering that Hindu-Muslim couples experience. She draws attention to how the “love jihad” “myth” has come to “define an entire community.” In an interview with The Diplomat’s South Asia editor, Sudha Ramachandran, Ara pointed out that while an interfaith relationship is a private matter between two people, “within the ‘love jihad’ narrative, the Muslim man is reimagined as part of a larger, organized project to convert Hindu women, increase the Muslim population, and eventually alter the country’s demographic and religious character.”
“Love jihad” is the idea that Muslim men are deliberately targeting Hindu women for relationships and marriage in order to convert them to Islam, and that this is part of a larger organized conspiracy. It is an elaborate example of political myth-making and what happens when paranoia about “Muslim danger” enters the mass psyche.
While doing fieldwork for my recent book, “Under a Saffron Sky,” what interested me was not only whether individual cases of deception or coercion exist — they can, as they do in any relationship — but how these individual cases are transformed into evidence of a larger, vast conspiracy, one that comes to define an entire community. The leap from “a Muslim man deceiving a woman” to “Muslim men are conducting an organized campaign against Hindu women to take over this country” is the crucial political leap. When it becomes part of a larger conspiracy, the myth then becomes powerful enough to shape families, communities, police action, and even public policy, acquiring a life of its own, with its own set of myths.
There have been cases such as the 2023 Purola episode in Uttarakhand, where an alleged attempt to abduct a 14-year-old girl was quickly branded as “love jihad,” triggering communal protests and the exodus of Muslim families. The case later collapsed in court, with the girl and her uncle contradicting the initial police version. The minor also told the court that police had tutored her to make allegations against the accused, who were subsequently acquitted.
Could you share with us an example of what an interfaith couple undergoes when they are accused of “love jihad”? 
Once people believe the myth of “love jihad,” real couples have to live with its consequences. One of the stories I reported from Uttar Pradesh is of a Hindu woman and a Muslim man who got married. After their nikah (wedding), when the couple went to the district magistrate’s office for their marriage registration, the man was shot in the head by two unidentified assailants right outside the government office in broad daylight. The couple wanted to register their marriage, make it official so no harm could touch them. But the woman saw her husband die before her eyes, minutes before that.
What made the story particularly chilling is the context. The couple had received warnings for weeks and months from local right-wing outfits and people opposed to the relationship and believed that once they had an official stamp from the government, no harm could touch their marriage. So, what began as a deeply personal decision, two people deciding to marry, gradually becomes something that others felt entitled to intervene in, threaten, and violently police.
In another example, from Gujarat, a state still scarred by the communal violence of 2002, a stamp vendor who had sold the couple their marriage stamps went on to call the woman’s family to inform them of their daughter’s “misdoings,” escalating the tension further.
In your book, you argue that “love jihad” is all about controlling women. Could you explain how?
One of the book’s main premises is that this is ultimately about controlling women, and that control operates across communities, although in very different ways. When a Hindu woman is told that she cannot choose her own partner because he belongs to another faith, her agency is being taken away. She is often treated as someone who has been deceived or brainwashed rather than as an adult capable of making a decision. But I also looked at Muslim women in the book. There is a case of a Muslim woman whose parents oppose her marriage because the man she has chosen was not just Hindu, but also belonged to a lower caste. The woman was told by her family that they might have considered a Hindu man — but only if he was upper caste. So, the policing of women’s choices isn’t confined to one community.
It’s an old story of women’s choices being made to represent the honor of an entire community, but what is distinctive about the “love jihad” campaign specifically is the way the Hindu woman has increasingly been made into a symbol, used as a tool, almost as the keeper of her entire community’s honor, purity, and demographic future. Her personal choices are seen as a collective threat. She is considered incapable of making her own decision, but in reality, her decision is powerful enough to threaten the demographic future of an entire community.
Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which includes an individual’s freedom to choose whom they wish to marry. In reality, less than 3 percent of marriages in India are actually interfaith, so this has never been an easy choice. It has always meant navigating disapproving parents, nosy neighbors and hostile looks. But increasingly, crossing that boundary can also mean the police coming to your home. These single-digit marriages are framed as “dangerous” or as something that could alter India’s demography.
“Love jihad” is fundamentally a threat-based concept: it brings together anxieties around women, community honor and national security. But what about the real wars being fought by women? The opposite can be opportunity-based concepts, focusing on potential gains, growth, and positive outcomes rather than on “avoiding dangers or risks.” We must look at the basics that affect the majority of our country’s women, from the girl child being killed to girls not getting education or healthcare access.
Could you share with us how right-wing organizations mobilize and prevent interfaith marriages?
The “foot soldiers,” as well as organizations that work around “love jihad” cases, have multiple sources of information and multiple ways of mobilizing. Some maintain strong local networks; others are highly visible on the street, actively watching for such cases. In some places, they don’t even need to go looking. They have become such recognized “authorities” that people from neighboring areas approach them directly to report what they see as suspicious behavior, or word that a Muslim man is trying to “lure” a Hindu woman.
There are also rehabilitation programs aimed specifically at women, meant to remind them of their religious identity and, in the language of these organizations, to “correct” or undo the ideological influence they are believed to have absorbed from Muslim men. It is not one form of mobilization but many: surveillance, family pressure, public intervention, ideological programming, and street action. Together, they create an environment in which an interfaith relationship becomes something the wider community feels entitled to police.
The Special Marriage Act of 1954 was supposed to help interfaith couples marry. Why hasn’t it worked?
A law can create a legal route, but societal adoption of that route is equally important. The Special Marriage Act was meant to allow people of different faiths to marry without requiring either person to convert. But over the years, interfaith marriage has become increasingly politicized, particularly when it involves a Hindu woman and a Muslim man. The problem is that couples aren’t operating in a social vacuum. They have to navigate families, communities, local officials, and, increasingly now, political scrutiny. A legal provision cannot by itself remove the social stigma or the fear surrounding the choice. The Special Marriage Act exists, but the real question is whether people feel genuinely safe to use it. What do couples do when the law gives you a right, but the process through which you exercise that right can expose you to physical, mental, emotional and legal risks?
Allegations of “love jihad” are usually hurled at Muslim men marrying Hindu women. Are such allegations levelled against Muslim women marrying Hindu men?
Yes, there have been cases where Muslim women have faced similar allegations, particularly allegations that they were attempting to convert Hindu men through marriage. In Uttar Pradesh, for instance, there have been cases where criminal complaints under anti-conversion laws were filed against Muslim women and their male relatives, with families alleging that conversions were being orchestrated through the promise of marriage. In some cases, Muslim women have even been sent to custody in connection with such allegations. So, the idea of a Muslim woman being an agent of conversion is certainly present in some cases.
If religious conversions did not happen, would anxieties that fuel “love jihad” allegations reduce?
Conversion sits at the center of the “love jihad” narrative, but I don’t think its absence would make the deeper anxiety disappear. One thing that became clear to me while reporting these stories is that suspicion often exists even where no conversion has taken place at all. A Hindu woman simply being in a relationship with a Muslim man can be enough to trigger the allegation of “love jihad.” There has been no substantial body of cases establishing an organized “love jihad” conspiracy behind forced conversions. Individual cases of coercion or deception can occur, of course, and deserve to be investigated on their own merits, but that is a very different thing from proving a larger, organized conspiracy.
What happens, then, is that the political idea becomes much larger than the evidence behind it. I sometimes think of it like Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein’s monster: something that is created and then acquires a life of its own. The narrative begins to generate its own evidence. An interfaith relationship becomes suspicious because people have already been told what such a relationship means; the absence of conversion does not necessarily dispel the suspicion. So, conversion is important to the mythology, but it is not really the whole story. The deeper anxiety is about the crossing of community boundaries through intimacy and marriage. Who is allowed to love whom? What happens when a woman chooses a partner from another community? What religion will the children follow? Will the family retain its religious identity? And that is why I see “love jihad” as part of a larger politics of controlling women’s choices.
The policing of interfaith marriage exists across communities. Muslim women too can face enormous family and social pressure when they marry outside the community. But “love jihad” has given that anxiety a particularly powerful political vocabulary when the relationship is between a Hindu woman and a Muslim man.
The Christian Church in Kerala has also accused Muslims of “love jihad.” How similar is their campaign against interfaith marriage?
While there are similarities, there are also important differences. The similarity is in the underlying anxiety: the fear that women from one’s own religious community are being targeted by men from another community, and that such relationships could lead to conversion, loss of community identity, or demographic change. But the Christian discourse in Kerala has been more localized and has emerged from a very different social and political context, rooted largely in concerns within the Christian community about young women, interfaith relationships, and conversion.
The “love jihad” narrative in the wider Hindu nationalist discourse, on the other hand, has acquired a much larger political vocabulary. It has been linked not just to conversion and interfaith marriage, but also to concerns about demography, population growth, religious identity and, at times, national security. It has therefore travelled far beyond individual relationships and become part of a broader political narrative. These campaigns may emerge from different contexts, but they draw upon an older anxiety around women, sexuality and community boundaries.
So I would say the resemblance is real, but the scale, impact, context, and political consequences are different.
articles.summary: Ara explains the insidious harm of the “love jihad” myth: “A deeply personal decision, two people deciding to marry, gradually becomes something that others felt entitled to violently police.”

articles.title: Why Pakistan Turned on the Taliban (and Vice Versa)
articles.full_text:
Why did Pakistan declare “an open war” against its one-time protégé?
On the night of February 21, 2026 Pakistan launched air and missile strikes on three border provinces in Afghanistan. What was Pakistan bombing? Suspected camps of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan – the TTP for short – and the Islamic State of Khorasan Province. 
The Taliban regime in Afghanistan retaliated by hitting Pakistani border posts. 
Pakistan then upped the ante. Its military launched Operation Ghazab Lil-Haq — which means Righteous Fury — against Afghanistan. 
“Our patience has now run out. Now it is open war between us,” Pakistan’s defense minister said on February 27. 
Pakistan and Afghanistan have engaged in numerous strikes and counter-strikes in the months since. While these have declined in frequency and magnitude, thanks to mediation efforts by China, the military strikes were still happening into September 2026. TTP attacks in Pakistan have also continued. 
Few would have expected Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban to turn on each other. They had been close allies for over 30 years – through the Taliban’s entire existence. When the Taliban captured power in Kabul in August 2021, Pakistan celebrated. 
So why did Pakistan declare “an open war” against its one-time protégé? Is there more to Pakistan’s military strikes on Afghanistan than taking out TTP camps? And can the Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship be salvaged?

articles.title: Indonesia Finally Has Its Aircraft Carrier. Now Comes the Hard Part.
articles.full_text:
Following a controversial acquisition, the most pressing question is whether and how Indonesia can convert the vessel into a viable military asset.
The Italian aircraft carrier ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, now the KRI Sriwijaya of the Indonesian Navy, steams through the Atlantic Ocean while participating in Majestic Eagle 2004, July 12, 2004.
Last year, reports surfaced that Indonesia was considering acquiring an aircraft carrier for the first time in its history. This prompted a heated debate over whether Indonesia truly needed an aircraft carrier. In an article published in The Diplomat, I argued that Indonesia didn’t need such an acquisition, at least for the time being, for a variety of reasons. The arrival of the KRI Sriwijaya, as the new vessel is known, thus marks the end of one discussion and the start of another. The key question now is whether Indonesia can turn the ship into a sustainable military capability.
On September 18, the aircraft carrier, formerly known as ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, arrived at Tanjung Priok Port in Jakarta. The ship was personally welcomed to port by the minister of defense, the commander of the Indonesian National Armed Forces, and the chief of naval staff. A formal handover from the Italian Navy to the Indonesian Navy took place on September 24, at which the carrier was reflagged and christened with its new name,
The name chosen by the Indonesian government has important symbolic importance. Sriwijaya was a strong monarchy and a respected naval power in Sumatra from the 7th to the 13th centuries.
However, with the ship’s arrival, the most important question is whether and how Indonesia can convert the ship into a viable military asset?
Aircraft carriers are often associated with naval superiority. Their ability to carry and operate aircraft or helicopters from the sea provides flexibility in projecting power, extending a navy’s range of operations, while also offering strategic options that do not entirely depend on land-based airfields. Moreover, the possession of an aircraft carrier with its various strategic values also brings prestige.
However, an aircraft carrier is not an arms technology that can produce strategic effects independently. Like other conventional weapon technologies, the effectiveness of an aircraft carrier heavily relies on the supporting ecosystem that enables it to operate sustainably and safely. In general, aircraft carriers never sail independently. In operation, the aircraft carrier will be part of a carrier strike group (CSG), which usually consists of an aircraft carrier, a guided missile cruiser, anti-aircraft warships, and anti-submarine destroyers or frigates. In carrying out its operations, the aircraft carrier is also often escorted by attack submarines.
The ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi was always escorted by other warships while still flying the Italian flag. For example, during the Passing Exercise in the Mediterranean Sea in 2020, Garibaldi was accompanied by at least two multirole frigates and one supply ship.
In a CSG, each element has a complementary function, ranging from air defense, anti-submarine warfare, protection of the aircraft carrier, logistics, to command and control. Therefore, the capabilities produced by the CSG are the result of the integration of various platforms, not merely a consequence of the presence of an aircraft carrier itself.
In the context of Indonesia, the issue of the availability of escort and support fleets for aircraft carrier operations becomes is a very important issue. Indonesia indeed now has its long-awaited carrier, but still lacks surface warships to form a CSG as commonly found in the United States or French navies. Referring to the Laboratorium Indonesia 2045 database, Indonesia still lacks 12 frigates and seven fast missile boats to fulfil the government’s Archipelagic Trident Shield defense posture goals. The same goes for the submarine fleet. Indonesia is recorded to still be short of at least eight submarines.
The government and the Indonesian National Armed Forces (TNI) have indeed stated on several occasions that the presence of KRI Sriwijaya is not intended for expeditionary combat missions. They argue that the aircraft carrier will instead be prioritized for military operations other than war, specifically humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR). For instance, once operational, the government stated that KRI Sriwijaya would join other TNI forces to assist in handling the  ongoing forest fires in Kalimantan. In addition to HADR missions, the Indonesian Navy chief of staff has said that the carrier will be used for defense diplomacy activities, such as port visits.
At first glance, the government’s and TNI’s statement to prioritize HADR missions and defense diplomacy for KRI Sriwijaya sounds rational. Besides the fact that Indonesia’s military posture does not allow for offensive operations, this statement is also expected to prevent diplomatic tensions with other countries, especially in the region.
However, this again raises the question of whether Indonesia truly requires an aircraft carrier. HADR can be a relevant mission for KRI Sriwijaya, but the relevance of a mission does not automatically prove that the chosen platform is the most effective way to achieve that capability. To ensure that KRI Sriwijaya can fulfill its role, Indonesia must still build the right ecosystem around it. For example, if it is intended for HADR missions on land, then Indonesia must ensure the availability of adequate transport helicopters. If Indonesia does not invest in acquiring a sufficient number of transport helicopters, then the KRI Sriwijaya will only become a sitting duck in the middle of the Nusantara sea when a disaster occurs on land.
In other words, if Sriwijaya is to be used for HADR missions, the measure of its success should not stop at the ship’s ability to carry helicopters to disaster areas. A more important question is whether the entire ecosystem built around the ship produces HADR capabilities that are significantly higher than the simpler and more cost-effective alternatives. At this point, Indonesia needs to realistically define the capabilities that it actually wants to derive from Sriwijaya so that it can then build the appropriate ecosystem around it.

articles.title: The Islamabad Memorandum Returns to the Spotlight
articles.full_text:
For Pakistan, the coming days will test whether its mediation capacity can keep pace with a conflict that continues to expand in both geography and complexity.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif (left) shakes hands with Iranian President Dr. Masoud Pezeshkian at their meeting on the sidelines of the UNGA meeting in New York, Sept. 24, 2026.
The Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) that Pakistan helped negotiate between Iran and the U.S. in June and which had largely dropped out of public discussion in recent months is back in the news again. The renewed attention on the MoU, however, does not necessarily indicate a clear pathway toward a lasting de-escalation of the conflict. Rather, it signals a new high level of endorsement since its signing in June.
The Pakistan-mediated 14-point interim understanding that Washington and Tehran endorsed was intended to halt the armed hostilities, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and create space for broader talks on nuclear and other issues. Its recent return to high-level conversations during the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) summit in New York suggests that, despite repeated setbacks, the agreement still serves as the primary reference point for those seeking to prevent further escalation.
The latest references to the MoU emerged largely at meetings held on the sidelines of this year’s UNGA. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, speaking after discussions with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, stated that the entire Pakistani leadership remained united in its resolve to expedite the peace efforts outlined in the Islamabad MoU. Pezeshkian, for his part, reaffirmed that the memorandum remained “totally acceptable” to Iran and that Tehran was ready to take it forward. These remarks, delivered after weeks of relative quiet, signaled that both sides of the original mediation still viewed the document as a viable baseline for de-escalation.
Chinese President Xi Jinping added further weight to the MoU during his state visit to the United States last week. In talks with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House, Xi expressed support for the U.S. and Iran returning to the June deal that was meant to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. He also said that both parties should resolve differences through dialogue and negotiation and reach a comprehensive agreement that included the nuclear issue.
Amid this renewed focus on the June agreement, President Xi’s intervention carried particular significance because it came amid broader discussions on global economic stability. The Chinese leader also noted that new economic and trade arrangements between Beijing and Washington represented positive news for the economies and peoples of both countries and for the world economy at large. By linking regional de-escalation to the condition of the global economy, Xi underscored that the prolonged crisis in West Asia carries costs that go far beyond the immediate theater of conflict.
While these high-level statements are important, developments on the ground indicate that negotiations have not gathered significant momentum. For instance, Iranian officials held three hours of talks with U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of UNGA. This was the first such contact since U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance met an Iranian delegation in Switzerland in June to advance the memorandum. The meeting itself produced no public breakthrough, but its occurrence after months of silence suggested that channels remain open.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi injected urgency into these latest conversations by stating that if the necessary conditions were met, the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days. He emphasized that the actions required of the U.S. are already contained in the MoU and that the choice now resides with Washington.
Meanwhile, Trump has rejected the Iranian proposal for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, with some reports indicating that the U.S. is planning another round of attacks on Iran after the upcoming midterm elections. Meanwhile, Iranian officials appear to have ignored Trump’s rhetoric, saying that they are waiting for an official response from mediators on the proposals under discussion within the Islamabad framework.
For Pakistan, the renewed focus on the MoU offers another opportunity to press for de-escalation between Iran and the U.S., especially since the agreement now has Xi’s explicit backing.
However, the stakes for Islamabad have grown considerably since June. Pakistan is no longer focused solely on salvaging the original understanding. The country’s policymakers are simultaneously attempting to help ease tensions between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia as well as Iran and the U.S.
Last week, the military leadership from Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan convened under the joint Makkah defense pact to discuss urgent steps in support of the Saudis amid Houthi attacks. The three countries resolved to accelerate military cooperation, with Islamabad and Riyadh separately committing to joint efforts to confront threats to Saudi territory. This expanded mediation portfolio has arguably stretched Pakistan’s diplomatic capacity at a time when the original Iran-U.S. conflict has only broadened in scope.
Moreover, there are additional risks which can complicate the picture. For instance, Trump has reportedly hinted at the possibility of renewed military action against Iran even as de-escalation talks continue. Tehran has responded with warnings of new military surprises should it come under attack. Iranian officials have also cautioned that any future confrontation could extend the conflict into the Arabian Sea.
It is pertinent to mention that Pakistan possesses no enforcement mechanism within the Islamabad MoU. The country’s influence rests solely on the goodwill of the primary parties and the diplomatic capital it has accumulated through mediation efforts. As the war continues to stretch and new fronts are opening, there is a growing risk that the original understanding may be overtaken by events, which could put additional pressure on Islamabad’s carefully cultivated role as a regional mediator.
The Islamabad MoU has arguably returned to the diplomatic conversations not because its implementation is imminent, but because it remains the only structured framework both sides have formally accepted as part of a de-escalation mechanism.
Whether that framework can still function as a roadmap depends less on statements delivered in New York or Washington and more on the willingness of Iran and the U.S. to translate words into actions on the ground.

articles.title: Kim Aris On the Campaign to Free Aung San Suu Kyi
articles.full_text:
As Myanmar’s “parody democracy” seeks regional re-engagement, the whereabouts of the Nobel laureate remain a closely guarded secret.
Kim Aris poses in front of a portrait of his mother, Aung San Suu Kyi.
Kim Aris has conducted a concerted campaign for the release of his mother, Aung San Suu Kyi, ever since she was detained in early 2021, when Myanmar’s military ousted her elected government and tipped the country into a bloody civil war.
Her meeting last month with an official from the International Committee for the Red Cross, following Kim’s Proof of Life campaign, did little to calm fears for the Nobel laureate’s health and safety amid claims that the meeting was staged, and at this point her whereabouts remain a closely guarded secret.
Kim Aris spoke to The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt about his mother’s fate, the National Unity Government (NUG) in exile, and the ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) battling it out with the military in a conflict that has now killed more than 100,000 people.
He also talks about the recent diplomatic tour by the regime’s president Min Aung Hlaing to neighboring countries and his administration, which he described as a “parody of democracy,” since one-sided elections were held in January.
“Sometimes I think that a parody of democracy could be more dangerous than a blatant dictatorship, because that gives people an opportunity to avoid doing anything about it,” he said.
“Min Aung Hlaing claimed that Myanmar remains on the path to democracy. That’s just a calculated attempt to pacify domestic resistance and offer foreign governments an easy diplomatic off-ramp to normalize relations or justify inaction.”
He also discussed the recently formed Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union, which combines the NUG, key EAOs, and parliamentary bodies, describing it as an important step toward a genuine federal democracy in Myanmar.

articles.title: Assam Government Encroaches Into a World Heritage Site in India’s Northeast
articles.full_text:
The encroached area is part of Manas National Park’s core tiger and Bengal florican habitats.
Manas National Park in Mathanguri, India.
Manas National Park in the northeast Indian state of Assam is in danger. The Assam government, which should be protecting this 1,176-acre World Heritage Site, has encroached on the park for several years.
Originally part of the North Kamrup Reserve Forest, the land under contention, which is spread over 9.3 sq km, was given on a 30-year lease to the Indian government for setting up a seed farm. After the lease expired in 2001, the area became part of the Manas National Park and Tiger Reserve, the Assam forest department said in a letter to the Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) that governs this region.
In the letter, the Assam forest department pointed out that the BTC had leased the encroached land for cultivation. Sources claimed that local farmers are engaged in farming in the area, which is officially not permitted inside a wildlife sanctuary, national park or World Heritage Site. The letter made a case for its handover to the forest department. The forest department also urged the Assam government to convince the BTC to return the encroached area to the Assam forest department
The area that has been allegedly encroached by local farmers with the BTC’s consent is part of the Manas National Park’s core tiger and Bengal florican habitats. This falls in the Bhuyanpara Range of the park, which is also where the erstwhile government-owned Kokilabari Seed Farm was located.
Concerned about the encroachment and its devastating impact on the park, the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) has also been reminding the Assam government to initiate action over the past few years.
In a communique dated July 30, 2026, which was also posted on social media, the NTCA asked the chief secretary of the Assam government to “intervene” and facilitate the “handing over” of the encroached area to the Manas Tiger Reserve authorities. It also reminded the government that a directive on the issue had been sent on June 11, but the authority was “not aware about the progress made in the matter so far.”

articles.title: China Conducts Military Exercise in South China Sea After Confrontation at Disputed Shoal
articles.full_text:
The “provisional understanding” between Beijing and Manila over the Philippine resupply of Second Thomas Shoal appears to have broken down.
China’s military conducted a joint training exercise around the disputed Scarborough Shoal in the South China Sea, it announced yesterday, two days after the Philippines accused Beijing of obstructing a resupply mission in another part of the contested waterway.
The People’s Liberation Army Southern Theater Command said in a statement on WeChat that the combined air and naval drill was ⁠a necessary response to actions by “certain countries” that it said had undermined regional ​peace and stability, Reuters reported.
The exercise “aims to test and enhance combat capabilities in safeguarding China’s territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests,” the Southern Theater Command said.
The China Coast Guard announced separately that the exercises focused on “maritime rights-protection, law enforcement, and management and control” in the waters around Scarborough Shoal.
A triangular atoll that sits around 200 kilometers to the west of the Philippines’ Luzon Island and 874 kilometers from China’s Hainan Island, Scarborough Shoal has been a persistent flashpoint in the maritime disputes between the Philippines and China. The shoal has been under Chinese control since 2012, when the two nations engaged in a tense 10-week stand-off that concluded with China occupying the feature, despite an agreement for mutual withdrawal from the shoal.
Since then, China Coast Guard (CCG) vessels have surrounded the shoal and made repeated attempts to restrict Filipino fishermen from accessing the rich fishing grounds inside the atoll’s central lagoon.
While the Chinese military did not specify which “certain countries” were the pretext for the joint exercises, it is not hard to guess.
Two days earlier, Manila accused the CCG of obstructing a resupply ​mission to troops stationed at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands, prompting a strong rebuke from the Chinese government.
In a statement on Friday, Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson Jay Tarriela said that the mission, which aimed to resupply the troops stationed aboard the BRP Sierra Madre, the grounded warship that functions as Manila’s foothold on the shoal, was “temporarily suspended after a CCG vessel carried out dangerous maneuvers” against the Philippine resupply vessel M/V Lapu-Lapu. The maneuvers “put Filipino personnel at risk” and prevented the mission from being completed, he said.
“There was ​no collision, and no one was injured, but the ​dangerous maneuvers of the China Coast Guard created a serious ⁠risk of collision,” Tarriela added.
For its own part, CCG spokesperson Jiang Lue accused the PCG of engaging in “provocative” acts at Second Thomas Shoal, restating its position that the BRP Sierra Madre was illegally grounded on the shoal in 1999.
“China Coast Guard, in accordance with the law, took measures including on-site monitoring and following, as well as issuing verbal warnings to the Philippine resupply vessel,” it stated. It added that the CCG “will resolutely safeguard China’s territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests.”
In a statement, the U.S. embassy in Manila condemned the Chinese action and lauded its Philippine allies’ “professionalism and restraint.”
“The United States strongly condemns the use of dangerous blocking and other irresponsible maneuvers by the China Coast Guard and the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) that threatened a collision with a Philippine vessel and prevented a lawful and routine resupply mission to Second Thomas Shoal,” it said.
In what has now become a predictable pattern, the Chinese embassy responded by condemning the U.S. for its “insistence on supporting the Philippines’ provocative and unlawful actions at Ren’ai Reef.”
“China urges the U.S. side to stop fanning the flames and refrain from actions that undermine regional peace and stability,” it said.
Friday’s incident comes just over two months after a serious confrontation at Second Thomas Shoal, in which a Philippine Navy marine sustained a head injury after being struck with a baton by CCG personnel, who were taking photos and videos of the grounded warship.
This broke a period of relative calm at Second Thomas Shoal, following a string of increasingly dangerous confrontations between the two sides in 2023 and 2024. These incidents, which stemmed mostly from Chinese attempts to prevent the resupply of the Philippine forces aboard the BRP Sierra Madre, culminated in a July 2024 melee between the CCG and PCG that left eight Philippine naval personnel injured, including one who lost a thumb in the fighting. The two sides subsequently agreed to de-escalate the situation at Second Thomas Shoal, reaching a “provisional understanding” that allowed the Philippines to resupply the grounded warship.
Friday’s interdiction attempt suggests that this “provisional understanding” between Manila and Beijing has now broken down, potentially ushering in a new period of tension at Second Thomas Shoal.

articles.title: Another Lao Activist Vanishes in Thailand
articles.full_text:
Khieo Lapchanh is the latest Lao exile to fall victim to the growing authoritarian collaboration between the Mekong region’s governments.
A photo of Khieo Lapchanh, a dissident Lao exile, that was posted on his Facebook page on Mar. 20, 2026.
In the early hours of September 15, Khieo Lapchanh, a 26-year-old Lao content creator, finished his shift at a restaurant in Thailand’s Samut Sakhon province and vanished. The following day, he was due at the Office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) for his first asylum registration interview. He never arrived.
Khieo came to Thailand in 2019 and late last year began posting Facebook videos sharply critical of the Lao government. Within months, his Khiew Channel Facebook page had amassed some 159,000 followers. Among his targets was the Siphandone dynasty, whose hold on high office runs from former president Khamtay Siphandone to his son, Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone, and his daughter, Vice President Viengthong Siphandone.
The backlash was swift. Khieo was doxxed, depicted in violent AI-manipulated content and subjected to death threats, including a $8,000 bounty on his life. Fearing for his safety after Lao officials twice visited his mother’s home, he withdrew from public activism. Silence, however, offered little protection.
Khieo is far from the first Lao dissident to vanish or die in Thailand while seeking UNHCR protection. In August 2019, Od Sayavong, a member of the Free Lao group, disappeared in Bangkok while awaiting resettlement to a third country, and Thai police concede that their investigation has made no progress. In May 2023, the body of Bounsuan Kitiyano, a UNHCR-recognized refugee and fellow Free Lao member, was found near the Lao border in Ubon Ratchathani province with three gunshot wounds. He had been planning to move to Australia, and no one has been held accountable for his killing.
The timing of these cases suggests that Lao authorities are closely monitoring activists’ engagement with UNHCR, and that they are prepared to use violence to stop their critics from reaching the safety of a third country.
These cases also expose Thailand’s failure to protect those seeking refuge within its borders. In a 2024 report, Human Rights Watch analyzed 25 cases of transnational repression in Thailand since the 2014 military coup, finding that refugees and asylum seekers have faced surveillance, violence, abductions, enforced disappearances, and forced returns facilitated by the Thai government. The report describes a “swap mart” in which foreign dissidents sheltering in Thailand are effectively traded for critics of the Thai government living abroad.
Thailand’s legal framework compounds this vulnerability. Because the country is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention, asylum seekers are treated as illegal immigrants and remain liable to deportation. In January 2022, another member of the Free Laos group, Khoukham Keomanivong, was arrested in Thailand for overstaying his visa (despite holding a UNHCR card) and only narrowly avoided deportation to Laos following intervention by civil society actors.
Responsibility for Khieo’s disappearance does not rest with Laos, or Thailand, alone. On September 23, just eight days after Khieo disappeared, more than 130 U.N. human rights experts issued a joint statement urging states to prevent and combat transnational repression and calling for expedited asylum, resettlement and humanitarian visa processes for those at risk. They also warned that such repression is increasingly digital, deploying social media, spyware and malware.
The cross-border targeting of activists is part of a broader global democratic retreat in which many states are culpable. Freedom House reports that global freedom declined in 2025 for the 20th consecutive year, while CIVICUS finds that just 7 percent of the world’s population lives in countries with open or relatively open civic space. Laos fares poorly on both, scoring 13 out of 100 in Freedom House’s index and rated “closed” by CIVICUS. Nor does the threat to Lao activists end at Thailand’s borders. In June 2025, exiled activist Joseph Akaravong was stabbed in the throat and torso in Pau, France, in what the local prosecutor described as an attempted assassination.
China has long been identified as a force for authoritarian consolidation in Southeast Asia and it is the largest source of development assistance and investment in Laos. But China is not the only country with responsibility to bear. In 2025, after Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency set its sights on USAID, the Trump administration cancelled 83 percent of the agency’s programs. Human Rights Watch reports that safe houses for at-risk human rights defenders in authoritarian countries have closed as a result. Manushya, the organization supporting Khieo, had relied on U.S. government funding to run nine safe houses for activists from neighboring states, including Laos and Cambodia, and its founder warned that without that funding it could no longer protect activists facing transnational repression. The sector is now understaffed and under-resourced, leaving activists less safe. The United States must reinvest heavily in human rights protection in Southeast Asia, and other democracies must increase their funding.
On November 24, Laos is scheduled to graduate from least developed country status, a milestone that will no doubt be marked with much fanfare. Yet it must not be forgotten that the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party has ruled for five decades without organized opposition, independent civil society or independent media, and that since Sombath Somphone’s shocking abduction in 2012, there have been at least 10 murders or attempted murders of Lao activists. Any celebration of the country’s graduation must be accompanied by this story.
Another accompaniment to the graduation toasts is a recognition that young Laotians are no longer willing to remain silent about the lack of freedom and opportunity in their country. Each dissident killed or disappeared only deepens convictions that activism is necessary. The party may continue to silence individual critics, but others will continue to speak out – and those who do not confront the government directly are protesting with their feet. Freedom House notes that Laos’ economic crisis has prompted growing youth emigration, with Lao nationals now the largest group using Thailand’s formal labor migration channel; they now total 267,871, or 40 percent of the total, a figure that continues to rise. In one Xayaburi district, 1,039 of 5,632 high school students dropped out in a single year to find work, and the true number of young Lao leaving is considerably higher once irregular migrants are counted. Their departure is a protest against a government that is failing to offer them a future.
The final lesson of Khieo’s disappearance is one for Lao activists themselves: they must build stronger solidarity. In May, a prominent U.S.-based Lao activist posted a video stating that Khieo was alive and working at a restaurant in Thailand, and shortly before he vanished, it was circulating online once more. This is not the first time an activist has been exposed in this way. When Anousa “Jack” Luangsuphom was shot in Vientiane in 2023, his family initially reported him dead, fearing that the gunman would return if he learned Jack had survived. Within days, news that he was alive in hospital became public and was shared online by a fellow activist. Rivalries and egos among Lao activists only undermine their shared cause and leave everyone less safe. To succeed, they will need to work together.

articles.title: Filipina Drug Trafficker Walks Free After Receiving Presidential Pardon
articles.full_text:
Mary Jane Veloso has always maintained her innocence, claiming that a relative tricked into carrying a large shipment of drugs.
A poster demanding the release of Mary Jane Veloso, as seen during a vigil in front of the Department of Justice in Manila, Philippines, July 10, 2015.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Friday granted a pardon ​to Mary Jane Veloso, who was serving a ‌prison sentence for drug trafficking in the Philippines after her arrest ​in Indonesia in 2010.
According to PhilStar Global, Gregorio Pio Catapang Jr., the director general of the Bureau of Corrections, “personally handed” Veloso a copy of the pardon and her official release, completing the procedures for her discharge. Earlier on Friday, Marcos confirmed to reporters that he had signed a pardon the day before, without elaborating.
Veloso, a 41-year-old domestic worker and mother of two, was arrested in Yogyakarta in 2010 for trying to bring 2.6 kilograms of heroin into Indonesia. She was subsequently sentenced to death under Indonesia’s severe drug laws, but received a last-minute reprieve from execution in 2015 after Philippine officials asked then Indonesian President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo to let her testify against members of a prominent drug trafficking organization.
In December 2024, Indonesia agreed to repatriate Veloso after years of requests from the Philippines, where Veloso’s relatives and supporters had waged a persistent campaign for her release.
Veloso has always maintained her innocence, claiming that she was tricked into carrying the drugs by her godsister. She smiled as she left her prison cell in the Philippines on Friday, after more than 15 years behind bars. In a press conference with Catapang at the Bureau of Corrections, she held up the “absolute pardon” signed by Marcos, which removes the remaining legal consequences of her conviction, allowing her a fresh start, and offered a tearful thanks to the Philippine leader.
“I just want to tell our beloved President: Thank you so much for clearing my name and allowing me to return to my family,” she said, as per Inquirer.net. She added that she was looking forward to reuniting with her two sons, who have grown nearly to adulthood since her arrest.
“It was really hard being separated from them … I didn’t see my children grow, but I believe it’s not yet too late for me to be their guide,” Veloso said.
Veloso’s release was greeted with joy by family members and advocacy groups that have spent years campaigning for her release.
Veloso’s pardon marks a rare positive development in a story connected to Southeast Asia’s tough anti-drug regime. Indonesia is known particularly for its unforgiving approach to drug crimes, especially large-scale trafficking offenses.
Under the agreement Yusril Ihza Mahendra, then Indonesia’s senior minister for law and human rights affairs, said that the Philippines had agreed to respect the Indonesian court’s sentencing of Veloso and her status as prisoner in Indonesia.

articles.title: Mongolia’s New Government Set Ambitious Goals. But Are They Realistic?
articles.full_text:
Data centers, the Sovereign Wealth Fund, and a hydropower plant – will any of it better the lives of Mongolian people?
On September 15, Mongolia’s parliament, the State Great Khural, began its autumn session – and it started full throttle. The incumbent government headed by Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor has an ambitious agenda that saw it propose one of the largest state budgets. Among its goals: establishing a sovereign wealth fund, securing energy from China, and building data centers. Parliament will likely scrutinize many of these big initiatives. 
The State Great Khural has much to decide, but it is operating within a highly politically divided environment. Mongolia is still wrangling with government instability that began with the ousting of Oyun-Erdene Luvsannamsrai’s administration in June 2025. Uchral’s government only took office on March 31 of this year – less than six months ago.
When parliament convened on September 15, the new government revealed one of the largest state budget proposals in Mongolia’s history, asking for 41.3 trillion tugrik, with a deficit of 2.3 trillion tugrik. Economists and skeptics worry that, with inflation standing at 12.5 percent, such a large deficit will only increase Mongolia’s debt, forcing the government to increase taxes on businesses and individuals. The state budget proposal has already faced massive scrutiny within the parliamentary committees. In a warning sign for Uchral’s government, parliament failed to reach the required quorum last week. 
One of the major issues with the 2027 state budget proposal is the 2.3 trillion tugrik deficit. One of the solutions the Uchral government proposed is to utilize the increased Oyu Tolgoi dividend.  
On September 11, Mongolia and Rio Tinto agreed to amend the Oyu Tolgoi contract, the Shareholder’s Agreement that was first established 17 years ago. The amendment will allow Mongolia to receive 13 trillion tugrik, approximately $3.6 billion. Uchral also announced that Rio Tinto agreed to reduce operational costs by approximately 30 trillion tugrik, an equivalent of $8.4 billion. 
While the Mongolian parliament has to review another state budget amid the constant changes of government, a second issue that will face major scrutiny is the establishment of Mongolia’s Sovereign Wealth Fund. Under the Oyun-Erdene administration, in 2024, the Parliament of Mongolia passed new laws on a Sovereign Wealth Fund. In February 2026, just before it was forced from office, the Zandanshatar Gombojav government signed a preliminary agreement with companies to allocate 60 percent of the benefits from Mongolia’s strategic deposits to the Sovereign Wealth Fund as a new profit-sharing mechanism meant to benefit the public. 
The current trajectory and the goal of the Sovereign Wealth Fund, however, may have pivoted from Mongolia’s welfare system, which would have directly benefited the public. The fund is now leaning more toward a corporate governance structure. 
The initiative is now part of a larger reform in Mongolia’s state-owned companies. To support this reform, on September 10, Mongolia signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the U.S.-based BlackRock Financial Markets Advisory. BlackRock and the Mongolian government outlined a general framework that looks to explore selling shares in state-owned enterprises in both domestic and international capital markets. 
After the MoU was signed, critics asked whether BlackRock’s corporate model – the restructuring of Mongolia’s state-owned enterprises – aligns with the country’s semi-welfare system. The government will need to have access to those funds to provide public assistance to the elderly, the disabled, children, the poor, and for public education and health. These welfare systems are indeed at the heart of Mongolian society today. 
In 2025, Mongolia experienced intermittent protests and strikes from educators and medical workers, demanding a pay raise. If the Uchral government fails to deliver these promises, this wealth fund policy and priority changes will have a great impact on the Mongolian people who depend on these funds.  
Beyond the financial wrangling, the issue of energy security looms over Mongolia. The Iran-U.S. war has roiled global energy markets, as have repeated Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Mongolia is uniquely dependent on Russia for fuel, importing over 95 percent of refined petroleum products from its northern neighbor. When Russian supply dwindled, Mongolia felt the pinch. In the summer and fall of 2026, nationwide fuel shortages highlighted the country’s vulnerability and pushed policymakers to seek an additional source: China. In September, delegates from the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources held bilateral meetings with China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) to discuss importing 10,000 tonnes of refined petroleum, 4,000 tonnes of jet fuel, and 3,000 tonnes of diesel. 
Moreover, China is currently financing one of Mongolia’s first hydropower plants, Erdeneburen Project in Khovd province. With a Chinese soft loan line of approximately $288 million, the construction contract was awarded to Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) and PowerChina in 2023. 
In mid-September, Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa and officials inspected the progress on the construction of the Erdeneburen Hydropower Plant. The Office of the President announced that the project is now 40 percent complete. When finished, the plant will have the capacity to supply reliable electricity to five provinces, including Khovd, Bayan-Ulgii, Uvs, Zavkhan, and Govi Altai. 
Considering Mongolia’s energy infrastructure, combined with the landlocked challenges, full energy independence may not be in the cards as a short or medium term goal. That said, managing fuel shortages by reaching out to diverse global partners is in the national interest. Even prior to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Mongolia experienced intermittent energy shortages, which motivated the government to seek third-neighbor investments and diversify energy sources. 
In August, Mongolia’s Deputy Prime Minister Dorjkhand Togmid announced Mongolia’s interest in building data centers in connection with accelerating Mongolia’s renewable energy sources. While the initiative is an attempt to kill two birds with one stone, even before discussing investment opportunities, Mongolia will need to decide how to handle data centers’ demand not only for energy, but for water.
According to the Brookings Institution, “A typical data center uses 300,000 gallons of water each day… but large data centers can use an estimated 5 million gallons of water each day.” The study warned: “Building a new facility and pledging economic impact mean little without sustainably incorporating water resources into ongoing operations.” 
In 2025, an OECD study on water resources highlighted Mongolia’s water scarcity. Mongolia’s geographic disparities as well as surface water distribution make constructing – let alone maintaining – data centers a highly questionable endeavor. 
The Uchral government is viewing China’s data centers in Inner Mongolia as a template and following the global trend. However, despite the similarities in wind and solar capacity and the cold climate, the water issue is one of the most important areas that needs to be scrutinized before Mongolia moves forward. 
The State Great Khural has entered another highly politicized season with much to resolve. Unfortunately, the internal feud within the Mongolian People’s Party (MPP) will continue to weaken the parliament’s function. The MPP, the nominal ruling party with 68 total seats, is now effectively divided into two blocs of 30 and 38 legislators. 
The Uchral government’s proposals are supposed to bring Mongolia economic prosperity and development, but without truly addressing the long-standing challenges of corruption, air pollution, water shortages, and energy security, the people’s confidence in governance remains extremely fragile. What the Mongolian people need is lawmakers and a government that prioritize the well-being of its citizens – not political vendettas.

articles.title: China’s Visibility Gap Around the Trump-Xi Summit
articles.full_text:
Xi’s U.S. visit was extensively covered by official outlets. It’s much harder to gauge public opinion or even interest.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump shake hands during their summit at the White House, Sep. 24, 2026.
Beijing formally confirmed Chinese President Xi Jinping’s September 23-25 visit to the United States on September 21, just two days before the trip began. The news had barely registered among many of the Chinese people I spoke with the following day. Official coverage began appearing online following the announcement, but visible discussion among ordinary users on platforms such as Weibo, WeChat, and Xiaohongshu (RedNote) remained scarce.
That changed once Xi’s visit was underway. Chinese social media filled with reports about the summit, with much of the visible content coming from official outlets and accounts, emphasizing the diplomatic significance and choreography of the visit, including Trump’s reception of Xi and calls for “constructive strategic stability.” The shift from limited information to abundant official coverage raised a different question: How much did ordinary Chinese people know about the summit before official coverage moved into full gear?
On September 22, the day after Beijing’s formal announcement and one day before Xi’s visit began, I conducted informal interviews with a dozen individuals across China and the diaspora, including overseas students and professionals, domestic public-sector workers, private-sector employees, and an older relative. Awareness varied considerably by location and occupation. 
Overseas students and professionals had generally learned of the trip earlier through foreign news outlets or private messaging groups. Some public-sector employees in China learned about it only after the official announcement, noting that senior leaders’ schedules are typically kept confidential until the last minute. Meanwhile, many of the private-sector employees I spoke with in China remained unaware of the visit even after the announcement.
Yet when asked about it, many responded by searching for the news themselves. What they found was a remarkably uniform information environment. On Weibo, Douyin, and Xiaohongshu, searches related to Xi’s U.S. visit were dominated by official and state-media content. On Xiaohongshu, some targeted searches produced either zero visible results or unrelated posts concerning personal travel and visas. Under some official media posts, comment sections were restricted or turned off. The interviews suggested that curiosity could exist even when little of it was publicly visible.
It is tempting to attribute this lack of visible discussion solely to censorship, but the interviews pointed to a more complicated picture. One respondent pointed to self-censorship: “Some of what people might say in private wouldn’t feel appropriate to post publicly.” Others suggested that interest might increase only after the meetings produced concrete outcomes. 
The searches themselves could not reveal whether the lack of visible discussion reflected content controls, platform ranking, self-censorship, limited public interest, or some combination of these factors.
The summit itself added another layer to this ambiguity. Once Xi arrived in the United States, information about the visit was no longer difficult to find. Official reports and accounts circulated extensive coverage of the meetings and their diplomatic symbolism. Yet the greater volume of information did not necessarily make public opinion easier to observe: Much of what was readily visible still came from official sources rather than ordinary users.
However, in specialized, interest-driven spaces, discussion was easier to find. On WeChat financial blogs like “Liu Xiaobo Talk Finance” and their commentary threads, retail investors and market watchers debated the summit’s possible implications for tariffs, stock prices, and exchange rates. According to the CGCC-USA 2026 Business Survey Report, 79 percent of surveyed Chinese companies operating in the United States reported negative impacts from tariffs, while 36 percent anticipated a slight improvement in bilateral trade relations, underscoring the concrete economic stakes surrounding the summit.
The Trump-Xi summit thus exposed a broader “visibility gap” in China’s information environment. On September 22, even after the visit had been officially announced, many of the people I interviewed had not heard about it, although they often became curious enough to search once asked. Days later, information about the summit was everywhere, but the most visible narratives remained overwhelmingly official.
For outside observers trying to gauge public sentiment in China, the difficulty is not simply that Chinese people are silent. It is that the Chinese internet makes a lack of discussion unusually difficult to interpret.

Lina Ma is a Chinese-born freelance journalist and research writer based in New York. She covers gender, digital culture, and social change in contemporary China, She is also a contributing writer to Global Voices. articles.title: From Idols to KOICA: South Korea’s Disaster Support for Nepal
articles.full_text:
Pop star donations and state aid work together to give Seoul a durable bond with Nepal.
The Korea Disaster Relief Team (KDRT) deployed to Rasuwa, Nepal, to carry out search and rescue and emergency relief operations. after the devastating flood of Aug. 26, 2026.
Following the destructive August 26 floods in Nepal, Lee Know of the K-pop boy band Stray Kids donated 100 million won (about $72,600) through World Vision. After Lee Know’s donation, his bandmate Felix donated 50 million won (about $37,000) to the Korean Committee for UNICEF, specifically for Nepal flood relief, on his birthday. Stray Kids’ leader Bang Chan followed with a 200 million won (about $144,000) donation, giving half to the Korean Committee for UNICEF for Nepal flood relief and half to Seoul Rehabilitation Hospital. 
The gestures echo acts of support for Nepal by other Korean personalities in the past. For example, figure skater Kim Yuna and actor Lee Min-ho (a different celebrity from Lee Know, whose birth name is also Lee Min-ho) extended aid to Nepal after the devastating earthquake in 2015. 
For many Nepalis, this solidarity from Korean public figures has strengthened the goodwill between the two countries. Since diplomatic relations were established in 1974, Nepal-South Korea ties have grown through labor migration and an exchange of culture. 
At the time of his donation, Lee Know shared a message through World Vision Korea, which World Vision International Nepal passed on when I reached out to them. “I hope my support can offer some comfort and strength to those going through this difficult time,” Lee Know said. “I sincerely hope that displaced families and everyone working on relief efforts on the ground can return to their peaceful daily lives as soon as possible.”
According to World Vision International Nepal, Lee Know’s donation, along with other contributions, is helping it reach flood-affected communities in Rasuwa and Nuwakot. About 8,600 people have received emergency support so far, including food packages, shelter and hygiene kits, water tanks and pipeline support. Child friendly spaces have been set up for displaced children. Planned next steps include livelihood recovery, temporary learning centers, and restoring community health and water and sanitation facilities.
For Nepalis, the donations from Korean cultural icons have a special resonance.
“I felt really grateful. In Mahottari and Janakpur area we also face heavy floods every year, so when I saw a K-pop idol donated specifically for Nepal flood victims, it felt very personal. It feels like someone far away actually cares about us,” said Priyanshu Kumar Chaudhary, who is from Janakpur, in Nepal’s flood-prone Mahottari district.
Isha Shrestha, from Kathmandu, said her family wasn’t among those who suffered the most direct destruction. But, to her, the disaster still “felt very close” because of how deeply connected the capital is to the affected regions like Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading. When she shared the news of Lee Know’s donation with friends who don’t follow K-pop, she said, “They were genuinely surprised and appreciated that someone from Korea cared enough to support Nepal.” She believes that it’s a sign that such actions shape perceptions of South Korea “beyond K-pop and entertainment.”
But why do idols donate? Dr. Kaushal Kumar, chairperson at the Centre for Korean Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, believes that these gestures hold personal weight. Idols like Lee Know, he said, are driven by their humanitarian side. More specifically, they feel a sense of reciprocity toward their fans. In Kumar’s reading, the giving flows from the fandom itself, with the idols showing up for the people who consistently show up for them. 
“When I heard that Lee Know had donated 100 million won to help people affected in Nepal, I joined in with a small donation of my own,” a Stray Kids fan told the Korea JoongAng Daily on September 14. The fan said they chose to list the donor’s name as “Stay,” the group’s fandom name, giving as part of the fandom rather than as an individual. 
While celebrity giving is personal, emotionally resonant, and reaches Nepalis who might never read a bilateral aid agreement, state aid leaves lasting results as it helps rebuild hospitals and institutional partnerships. Chaeyoon Oh, an economic and development specialist at the Embassy of the Republic of Korea in Nepal, underscored South Korea’s role in the floods’ aftermath. She said that Korea deployed its Disaster Relief Team and sent DNA-identification experts. More recently, South Korea sent emergency equipment through the U.N. Development Program (UNDP) at the request of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. 
“To me, this goes beyond a government-to-government relationship,” Oh said. “It is an example of how people in one country can see the difficulties faced by people in another country and feel compelled to help.”
Dr. Dhruba Gautam, an expert associated with Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction Center (NDRC Nepal), confirmed that this Nepal-South Korea camaraderie is part of a larger track record. After the 2015 earthquake, South Korea’s aid agency, KOICA, provided $9 million to rebuild Trishuli Hospital and 10 health posts in Nuwakot. Following Nepal’s 2024 floods, South Korea gave $500,000 through UNICEF for medical tents and sanitation support. After this August’s floods, Seoul and the UNDP also supplied Nepal’s disaster authority with camera-equipped drones and portable generators for search and rescue. According to Gautam, South Korea’s clearest contribution has been through practical means such as the provision of equipment and health infrastructure. 
Roslyn Hanson Gabriel, national director of World Vision International Nepal, said that help from all sections of society is useful in combating natural disasters. “We are deeply grateful for the generosity and solidarity shown by supporters around the world, including Lee Know and many others who have stood with Nepal during this difficult time,” she said in a written response. “Contributions such as these help us reach children and families affected by the floods with urgent relief assistance while also supporting longer-term recovery efforts. Beyond the financial support, such expressions of global solidarity help shine a light on the needs of vulnerable communities and remind them that they are not facing these challenges alone.”
Diplomacy and culture reinforce the bond between two countries – with the help extended by individual personalities providing an emotional charge that state visits and MOUs find difficult to achieve, even though both work on building the trust between nations.
Both Chaudhary and Shrestha noted that gratitude for the aid is the beginning of a long journey to recovery. Chaudhary pointed to the persisting needs in his district: “We need long-term solutions like better river management, stronger houses, early warning systems. We are a strong community, we just need support to be more prepared.”
Shrestha put it directly when she said, “Thank you for standing with Nepal,” addressing Korean fans and celebrities. “But please remember us beyond the headlines. Long-term support for rebuilding communities and livelihoods can make an even deeper difference.”
This is a partnership that both governments and the general public on both sides seem intent on deepening. It’s the consistency that matters in connecting two nations in times of need. 
Comments from officials quoted in this piece were shared in their personal capacity. They do not necessarily represent the official positions of their respective institutions.
