articles.title: What Lies Behind the Rise in Anti-Israel Sentiment in Thailand?
articles.full_text:
Nationalist rabble-rousers have accused Israelis of trying to seize Thai territory, and Israeli tourists of misbehaving or disrespecting the country’s culture.
In this screenshot from a video posted on nationalist firebrand Sondhi Limthongkul’s YouTube channel, Thai nationalists participate in an anti-Israel protest outside the Israeli embassy in Bangkok, Thailand. Sep. 10, 2026.
For three years, small-scale pro-Palestine protests, centered around Israel’s human rights abuses in Gaza, have become common in Thailand. A few dozen left-wing activists would turn out to chant slogans more commonly associated with the massive street demonstrations in the West, to little interest from the general public or international media.
A few hundred protesters showed up at the Israeli embassy in Bangkok, with another 500 at the Chabad House in Phuket. These protests featured some explicitly anti-Semitic signs, like “Jews out,” and the protest in Phuket forced the cancellation of a small, private gathering for the Jewish New Year, due to security concerns.
“We are monitoring the situation surrounding the Jewish New Year event in the Patong area. These Jews are staying inside their mansions,” one protest organizer was quoted as saying by local media outlet Bangkok Post. The Chabad House did not respond to The Diplomat’s request for comment.
Left-wing activist groups said that these protests don’t represent them. Rather, the pro-Palestine cause has been hijacked by xenophobic far-right groups that also regularly target vulnerable migrant workers from neighboring countries.
The previous left-wing protesters had largely focused on Israel’s well-documented atrocity crimes against Palestinian civilians.
A Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023 left over 1,000 people dead in Israel, including 39 Thai migrant workers. Israel responded with a massive air and ground assault on the besieged Gaza strip, killing over 70,000 people, including over 20,000 under the age of 18. The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for crimes against humanity for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.
“At that time, the Israeli military began carrying out increasingly severe measures that went far beyond what could reasonably be described as mere ‘retaliation,’ as the Israeli government claimed. We saw these actions as part of a deliberate process of colonization,” said Nai, a protester who first became active in the pro-Palestine movement in late 2023, as a 19-year-old university student.
The Boycott, Divest, Sanctions (BDS) Movement in Thailand calls for the Thai government to stop sending Thai migrant workers to Israel, screen Israeli tourists and arrest those suspected of war crimes, end all arms trade and military agreements with Israel, and ultimately sanction Israel and sever diplomatic relations.
“BDS Thailand abides by the same values as the international BDS movement: freedom, justice, and equality. Thus, we oppose the bigoted, anti-Semitic, racist/xenophobic, and nationalist rhetoric that such right-wing opportunists espouse. BDS Thailand is NOT affiliated with and does NOT approve of right-wing demonstrations or their signage,” added the BDS Movement’s Thailand chapter.
The right-wing protesters have focused more on domestic issues, accusing Israel of trying to seize Thai territory, and Israeli tourists of misbehaving or disrespecting Thai people, allegations that have little empirical evidence to support them.
The land seizure allegation is rooted in an extremely common business practice in Thailand. Foreigners are prohibited from owning land, but many skirt this law by buying property through a company started with a Thai frontman – known locally as a “nominee.” This is done both to purchase private residences and launch small businesses, or at times for more large-scale real estate developments.
The government is cracking down on this practice, and some Israeli companies have been targeted. But Israelis are far from unique in this, and are unlikely to rank among the highest offenders.
The Ministry of Commerce released data on land owned by businesses with foreign investors, finding Chinese nationals held by far the most land, at around 35,000 acres, more than double the next nationality – Japanese. The United Kingdom, Singapore, and Hong Kong rounded out the top five, while the ministry said 147 nationalities own shares in companies that own land in Thailand.
(Not all of these companies would be illegal. The legitimacy of a business can be very hard to determine, because the main factor is whether the Thai business partner is a legitimate partner or just a frontman. The government says it is in the midst of a close review of suspicious businesses).
Accusations of Israelis misbehaving or disrespecting locals are harder to quantify. To be sure, there have been some viral incidents on social media, such as a young Israeli woman arrogantly claiming that “my money builds your country.” In another shocking episode, four Israeli men caused property damage and allegedly threatened staff at a hospital where a friend was receiving treatment following a motorbike accident.
Still, the vast majority of the 400,000 Israeli tourists who visited Thailand last year came and went without incident. Out of context social media clips hardly prove a statistical trend, but they have contributed to rising xenophobic sentiment the world over. Thai media outlets have seemingly realized that articles about Israelis generate high engagement, providing a steady churn of social media posts about even minor disputes or arrests.
An Australian national’s recent murder of a 17-year-old sex worker, meanwhile, did not provoke protests outside the Australian embassy. A massive influx of Russians to Phuket since the invasion of Ukraine has similarly not sparked protests, despite a rise in organized crime, including multiple high-profile incidents of kidnapping, extortion, and murder.
The anti-Israeli protests can be contextualized as part of a broader, growing anti-foreigner sentiment, that has targeted both unruly Westerners and vulnerable migrant workers.
When a group of Italian students insulted a Thai woman on a train in Bangkok, for example, a mob of protesters descended on their hotel, while the Italian embassy was flooded with angry comments on social media, though faced no in-person demonstrations.
The protester Nai said focusing on personal dislike of Israelis is a distraction from the issue at hand.
“From my perspective, although nationalist and right-wing groups have succeeded in turning opposition to Israel into a national-level issue and have brought some sections of the pro-Palestine movement into their demonstrations, this does not necessarily make the Palestinian cause itself a central political issue,” he said.
“If this movement were eventually to lead to a boycott of Israel, for example, the message communicated to both the international community and Thai society could simply become that ‘Israelis are bad,’ which is essentially a form of generalized racial prejudice,” he added. “What would be missing is the argument that a boycott of Israel should serve as a political statement to the international community: that Israel, which we see as a fascistic colonial state responsible for genocide, should face international pressure and consequences until genuine justice is achieved.”
Amid a floundering economy, others have directed this same xenophobic anger towards vulnerable migrant workers. Some 900,000 Cambodians were pressured to leave the country following border clashes last year, which also helped sweep the conservative, pro-military Bhumjaithai party to power at a general election earlier this year. With the Cambodians gone, migrants from Myanmar seem to be the next target, having sought refuge in Thailand by the millions amid a massive civil war back home.
Royalist activist Akkarawut Kraisrisombat, who organized the Chabad protest in Phuket, previously launched a 2024 campaign to deport pregnant migrant workers, though this failed to gain parliamentary support. He has since started a vigilante group called “Thais Won’t Tolerate” mainly focused on monitoring and reporting suspected illegal migrants, and has accompanied police on immigration raids.
Influencer Siranudh “Psi” Scott was present at the more recent, nationalist anti-Israel protests in Bangkok. He previously made waves when he accused foreign migrant workers who are unable to speak Thai of “taking advantage of our home.” In a social media post, he said if he goes to a restaurant and the staff speak to him in English, he will only speak Thai and request a new server. Many Burmese migrant workers in particular work in the service industry in Bangkok, and are often more proficient in English than Thai.
The Bangkok protest was led by Sondhi Limthongkul, an infamous conservative firebrand. Sondhi played a key role in destabilizing successive, democratically elected governments in 2006 and 2008, accusing them of undermining the monarchy, among other alleged malpractice. In 2008, Sondhi’s followers created a political crisis by occupying government buildings and an airport, giving an opening for the conservative establishment to wrest back control. While unproven, many have suspected Sondhi of colluding with the military to this end.
BDS Thailand said it is not affiliated with these right-wing activists or the ruling party, and accused “warmongering opportunists” of co-opting the pro-Palestine cause to “spread bigotry.” It added that the protests by Sondhi were “largely performative” and “unconnected to Palestinian liberation.”
While the recent anti-Israel protests were relatively small, the ruling Bhumjaithai party has ensured that the issue doesn’t remain on the fringes. The party seems happy to capitalize on rising anti-foreigner sentiment, having benefited enormously from the surge in nationalism during the war with Cambodia. Party leader and Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, also showed a degree of disdain for Westerners as health minister during the COVID-19 pandemic.
articles.summary: Nationalist rabble-rousers have accused Israelis of trying to seize Thai territory, and Israeli tourists of misbehaving or disrespecting the country's culture.

articles.title: North Korea’s Ukraine POWs Are Now in South Korea. What Comes Next?
articles.full_text:
Both the South Korean government and the two former soldiers face an unprecedented resettlement process.
The immediate fate of two North Korean prisoners-of-war captured by Ukrainian forces is no longer in question, but the saga is not yet over. 
Ukraine has transferred custody of the pair to South Korea in what was perhaps a predictable outcome given their reported desire not to return to North Korea. However, the circumstances surrounding the disclosure have introduced new political dynamics to the situation. Now, both the South Korean government and the two former soldiers face an unprecedented resettlement process.
Kyiv first announced that it had captured the two North Korean soldiers in January 2025, immediately prompting questions of what would come of the pair. The legal provisions surrounding their eventual disposition were complicated. International rules pointed toward repatriating them with other POWs to Russia. Before the capture happened, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was his government’s position that all POWs in Ukrainian custody would receive the same treatment.
The two soldiers, however, reportedly expressed fear of repatriation and a desire to defect to South Korea. Given the Kim Jong Un regime’s publicized insistence that soldiers kill themselves rather than be captured, returning to North Korea could have exposed them to reprisals for allowing themselves to be taken into Ukrainian custody. Under the principle of non-refoulement, the potential risk of persecution, torture, or other serious human rights violations if the soldiers were ultimately repatriated to North Korea was a necessary consideration.
The South Korean government stepped in early with offers to take the POWs into their custody. With advocacy stretching back to the previous Yoon Suk-yeol administration, there was little doubt over Seoul’s desired outcome for the two individuals.
What is now evident is that the two governments came to a confidential agreement to transfer the custody of the POWs. The handover reportedly took place ahead of the U.N. General Assembly debates, and the two former soldiers are now in South Korean government care. Details of this arrangement first came to light via Zelenskyy himself.
During his speech at the U.N. General Assembly, the Ukrainian president captured international attention when he revealed that Ukraine had transferred custody of the two POWs to South Korea. In the speech, he noted that “these guys are not easy to capture alive,” adding that one of the soldiers, “when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself.” Zelenskyy’s disclosure came unilaterally and without warning to the South Korean government.
Kyiv’s decision to reveal information despite the confidential arrangement created a diplomatic problem with Seoul, but it also served a clear Ukrainian purpose. Kyiv’s intelligence has repeatedly claimed that the Kremlin is seeking an additional 30,000-50,000 North Korean troops to support a new offensive. Zelenskyy therefore used the U.N. General Assembly debates as a platform to highlight the Kim regime’s continued support for Russia’s war effort and to put North Korea’s military involvement back on the international agenda.
But Zelenskyy’s announcement caused a stir in South Korean domestic politics. Opposition lawmakers immediately chastised the Lee Jae-myung administration for not disclosing the transfer. Some argued that the government was withholding details out of fear of how North Korea may react.
Lee took to social media to push back against this criticism. He said that there was an agreement to keep the transfer confidential, expressing that it was “deeply regrettable” that the Ukraine side released details on the matter. He added that publicly disclosing the successful repatriation could have helped boost approval ratings, but it would not have been right to risk “someone’s life or the national interest” for one’s “own petty benefit.”
There are political reasons why some in the Lee administration may have sought to avoid disclosing information about the POW transfer. The government has been working to rekindle any form of inter-Korean engagement, and some policy groups within Seoul have warned that North Korea could react strongly to the decision.
However, such concerns may be unfounded. North Korean state media has not commented on the POWs since their reported capture, and there are much more significant sticking points between the two Koreas; namely, Pyongyang’s preconditions that Seoul must drop unification and denuclearization as policy objectives. Since Zelenskyy’s announcement, the only reporting from Pyongyang directed toward the South Korean government has been a statement attributed to Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui on a familiar issue: reiterating the Kim regime’s position that denying the reality of North Korea’s nuclear weapon status “is to give up the future.”
Meanwhile, from a security perspective, there are justifiable concerns related to the information disclosure. There have been North Korean assassination attempts against South Korea-based defectors in the past. The most prominent recent example occurred in a 2011 incident in which a North Korean agent attempted to kill prominent defector-turned-activist Park Sang-hak with a poison needle. 
The two POWs could therefore present a different security challenge from the average North Korean defector. Their firsthand knowledge of North Korean involvement in the Russia-Ukraine War means that there is a reasonable risk that they could become targets of elimination efforts.
Given the confidential nature of the South Korea-Ukraine agreement, there are few details on what comes next for the two former soldiers. There may have been an understanding that they will remain in custody until the conclusion of the war, or Kyiv may have conceded that South Korea can treat the individuals as they would any other defector. This would affect how long the individuals remain in the government’s custody.
Whatever the length of their initial detention in South Korea, the eventual next step will be resettlement.
Resettlement can be difficult for any defector. New arrivals generally undergo a months-long program at the Hanawon resettlement facility under the Ministry of Unification’s remit, and it includes tasks such as teaching individuals about South Korean customs and courtesies, how to manage bank accounts and finances, and finding employment. 
Upon completion of the resettlement process, they are then given relocation assistance to a new residence somewhere in the country. There, they are typically assigned a local officer – either a Ministry of Unification, Korean National Police, or National Intelligence Service (NIS) official – to continue supporting their transition process and to contact in the event of any issues.
The system is different for higher profile or high-risk defectors. They may be former senior North Korean officials like Thae Yong Ho, or figures such as Park Sang-hak who have used their newfound freedom to lead civic movements in protest of the Kim regime. In those cases, the individuals can remain in NIS protective custody until officials determine that it is safe for them to return to public life. Even then, there may be continued protection services.
The two former soldiers transferred from Ukraine will likely fall into that latter category, particularly with the amount of media coverage they have received.
Thus, the arrival of the two North Korean soldiers to South Korea resolves the most immediate question surrounding their fate, but the next steps remain dynamic. The situation has now entered a new phase where South Korean politics will continue to scrutinize the issue as the government works to navigate an unprecedented resettlement process.

articles.title: The Militarization of Outer Space: Chinese Infrastructure in the Global South
articles.full_text:
Projects developed within bilateral frameworks could form an international infrastructure that provides China with operational advantages in space.
The militarization of space encompasses not only the deployment of weapons in space but also the potential military use of the space domain, including ground-based infrastructure. Most studies on the militarization of space limit themselves to analyzing the actions of major powers in the space sector, primarily focusing on the space race between the United States and China. 
While it’s true that China’s space program has positioned the country as the second global power in space, it’s important to note that Beijing’s main strategies include investments, innovation, and expanding collaboration with countries in the Global South. This strategy generates commercial benefits and seeks to create diplomatic coalitions that strengthen China’s influence in international institutions. It also allows China to establish ground-based and satellite infrastructure in regions such as Latin America and Africa. Given this development, questions arise about whether China’s bilateral satellite cooperation and associated infrastructure with Global South countries are part of a broader Chinese international infrastructure and the strategic implications this could have for the United States.
Since the 1980s, China has maintained partnerships with countries in the Global South in the satellite sector. In 1984, China began collaborating with Brazil in this sector, formally launching the China-Brazil Earth Resources Satellite (CBERS) program in 1988. Later, China expanded collaboration to other Latin American countries, including Venezuela, Bolivia, Argentina, and Chile. Since 2001, China has extended its partnerships to include countries in Africa. It established its first ground station in Swakopmund, Namibia and has since grown its satellite and infrastructure cooperation to include Nigeria, Egypt, Algeria, Ethiopia, and other countries in the region.
These collaborations include selling and jointly constructing communications and Earth observation satellites; constructing receiving and control stations, assembly and integration centers; offering personnel training programs; providing financing; and establishing mechanisms for scientific and technological cooperation. China frames these collaborations as part of its efforts to promote social and economic development in these regions while simultaneously combining commercial interests with enhancing its strategic capabilities.
We should not assume that the analyzed facilities or satellites are being used for military purposes. But we should pay attention to their potential dual use and the capabilities their combination could provide China. Considered collectively, for example, that the ground infrastructure in Argentina, Namibia, Ethiopia, Egypt, and other countries can provide greater geographic coverage and expand opportunities for telemetry, tracking, and command (TT&C) functions. It can also reduce latency in data reception and facilitate data distribution. Furthermore, integrating them with other systems could contribute to space situational awareness (SSA) and expand capabilities for tracking space objects.
Recently, U.S. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink confirmed that the United States has “space control weapons” deployed in space. This is an example of the trend toward the militarization of space, an area in which China and Russia have also demonstrated capabilities. In 2007, China tested its anti-satellite (ASAT) system, destroying one of its own satellites. This maneuver surprised Americans due to the technology China developed and the significant amount of debris produced by the collision. Additionally, India conducted an ASAT test in 2019, and Russia did the same in 2021. Other nations, such as Australia, France, Japan, Iran, Israel, North Korea, South Korea, and the United Kingdom, are developing counterspace technologies. With the growing number of actors, increasing development of kinetic and non-kinetic weapons technology, and reliance on the space domain for troop deployment and intelligence gathering, the militarization of outer space seems inevitable. The question here is what strategic advantages China’s growing space infrastructure in the Global South could provide.
Among other examples, two ground stations in Namibia demonstrate varying degrees of control over the space system. The Windhoek ground data receiving station, which opened in February 2026, was designed to receive and process data from remote-sensing satellites. According to the Chinese ambassador to Namibia, Namibian personnel will manage this ground station. However, Chinese personnel will remain on site to provide ongoing technical support to the technicians they have trained. Additionally, the station receives data from CBERS-4, combining data reception and processing with Chinese technical support and data reception from a Sino-Brazilian satellite.
The Swakopmund station, which was also built by China in Namibia in 2001, provides TT&C. It can also be used to track satellites flying over the South Atlantic. It is managed directly by the Xi’an Satellite Control Center, which is linked to China’s military space structures. While the Windhoek station focuses on receiving and processing Earth observation data, the Swakopmund station provides satellite TT&C capabilities.
China has even donated a satellite to Ethiopia. The ETRSS-1 is Ethiopia’s first remote sensing satellite. DFH Satellite Company Ltd., a subsidiary of the China Academy of Space Technology (CAST), designed and developed the satellite. CAST is a subsidiary of the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), which is part of China’s space and defense industrial system. Since 2012, the Entoto Observatory & Research Center has operated as a ground station in Ethiopia. The Entoto Observatory is a multisatellite ground receiving station that supports ETRSS-1 operations. It also receives data from other satellites, including CBERS-4, Gaofen-1, Gaofen-3, Gaofen-5, and GaoJing-1. The latter are Chinese satellites. Entoto has had a new antenna since 2025 that is responsible for ingesting high-resolution imagery.
China’s collaboration with Egypt is also noteworthy. China funded and helped build the MisrSat-2 Earth observation satellite, which was launched in late 2023. China also constructed the Satellite Integration, Assembly, and Testing Center (AITC) near Cairo. Thus, their cooperation encompasses earth observation, ground stations, TT&C, data applications, and satellite assembly, integration, and testing capabilities. China has access to shared ground laboratories and data processing centers in Egypt. This enables China to expand its international satellite image analysis infrastructure in a geopolitically sensitive region such as the Suez Canal.
The deep-space tracking station in Neuquén, Argentina, is the most prominent example of a Chinese ground station located outside of China with dual-use potential. Established through agreements between the National Commission for Space Activities (CONAE), the China Satellite Launch and Tracking Control General (CLTC), and the Neuquén provincial government, it features a 35-meter antenna and operates in the S, X, and Ka bands. It supports the Chinese lunar program and provides TT&C services. Its technical characteristics could enable dual-use applications, including satellite monitoring, intelligence gathering, and the interception of satellite signals, depending on the capabilities employed. Additionally, the station has institutional ties to the CLTC and the Xi’an Satellite Control Center. 
Together, the reception of the Sino-Brazilian CBERS-4 satellite at facilities in Africa such as Windhoek, the multisatellite capacity at Entoto, the TT&C station in Swakopmund, and the deep-space station in Neuquén demonstrate that projects developed within bilateral frameworks can have functional connections that extend beyond bilateral collaborations with China. These facilities could form an international infrastructure that would provide China with operational advantages in terms of geographic coverage, data reception and distribution, TT&C, and tracking space objects in regions such as the South Atlantic, the Mediterranean, and various areas of the African continent. Integrating these capabilities could contribute to broader Space Domain Awareness (SDA). Both the United States and Europe should examine the potential strategic implications of this infrastructure more systematically.

The militarization of space encompasses not only the deployment of weapons in space but also the potential military use of the space domain, including ground-based infrastructure. Most studies on the militarization of space limit themselves to analyzing the actions of major powers in the space sector, primarily focusing on the space race between the United States and China. 
While it’s true that China’s space program has positioned the country as the second global power in space, it’s important to note that Beijing’s main strategies include investments, innovation, and expanding collaboration with countries in the Global South. This strategy generates commercial benefits and seeks to create diplomatic coalitions that strengthen China’s influence in international institutions. It also allows China to establish ground-based and satellite infrastructure in regions such as Latin America and Africa. Given this development, questions arise about whether China’s bilateral satellite cooperation and associated infrastructure with Global South countries are part of a broader Chinese international infrastructure and the strategic implications this could have for the United States.
Dr. Ana Soliz de Stange is a researcher and lecturer at Helmut Schmidt University – University of the Federal Armed Forces Hamburg, Germany. She holds a Ph.D. from the University of Hamburg. Her research focuses on international relations, with particular emphasis on triangular relations involving Latin America, China, and the United States.
articles.summary: Projects developed within bilateral frameworks could form an international infrastructure that provides China with operational advantages in space.

articles.title: Taiwan Isn’t Giving Up, It’s Pulling Apart
articles.full_text:
Rising passivity in Taiwan doesn’t mean Taiwanese have given up on resisting. It means the conditions for political action are eroding.
A KMT-led rally on July 20, 2025, urges a “no” vote in the July 26 recalls.
In a recent article for The Diplomat, Mor Sobol offered an even-handed assessment of the debate set off by Simon Shuster’s piece in The Atlantic, which asked whether Taiwan might simply “give up” under growing pressure from China. Sobol argued that both Shuster’s pessimistic answer and his critics’ confident rebuttals rest on thinner evidence than either side recognizes. 
Sobol pointed out that telling a pollster “I would defend Taiwan” is very different from making that decision when missiles are falling, and that Taiwan is not a unitary actor. The question worth asking is how the trends in public opinion, military recruitment, defense spending and other metrics move over time, not what any single snapshot shows.
I agree. As a scholar who studies Taiwanese defense attitudes with survey data, I want to add evidence showing why the much-discussed “willingness to fight” has, to some degree, misled outside observers. The problem with polling is not that attitudes can’t be measured. It’s that pollsters keep asking the most superficial question. “Would you fight?” captures a sentiment. What decides whether that sentiment translates into action is whether citizens believe the conditions for sacrifice are in place. Those conditions can be measured, tracked over time, and broken down by group. 
When we do that, the picture is more troubling than either the optimists or the pessimists suggest, though for different reasons.
Citizens never accept the risks of war unconditionally. They take part in what I call a Defense Social Contract, which rests on three pillars, all of them vitally important.
The first pillar is trust in the state. People will sacrifice for a government they believe governs competently and fairly, and for a country they believe has a future worth defending. When citizens feel the state has failed them, its claim to extraordinary sacrifice loses legitimacy.
The second pillar is trust in one another. Defense is a public good, and public goods invite free-riding. I will hold the line only if I believe my neighbors will too. That means the burden must be shared, rather than some Taiwanese being expected to serve while others are exempt. Resistance must also be the common cause of all Taiwanese, not the property of one political camp.
The final pillar is trust that resistance can work. Facing a far more powerful adversary, citizens of a small democracy must believe their own military is capable and that allies will arrive in time. Sacrifice that looks futile turns into fatalism.
If any one pillar gives way, professed willingness to fight stays a sentiment and never becomes action.
All three pillars can be measured. To do so, I used two nationally representative waves of the Taiwan National Security Survey (TNSS), fielded in June 2024 and September 2025, with 2,745 respondents in total. This makes it possible to do what Sobol recommends: track change over time and look inside the aggregate. The timing deserves emphasis. The 2024 survey was fielded about a month after President Lai Ching-te took office. The 2025 survey was fielded about a month after the final round of Taiwan’s Great Recall votes, a national effort to recall all legislators from the Kuomintang (KMT) that ultimately failed.
The TNSS directly asks respondents what they would actually do if China invaded. One option is to “let nature take its course” (shun qi zi ran). That answer is not surrender, and it is not a rejection of Taiwan. It is withdrawal: wait and see. I call it fatalistic passivity. Between the two waves, the share of Taiwanese choosing it rose from about 26 percent to nearly 37 percent.
From 2024 to 2025, the TNSS results showed that all three pillars weakened or came under strain.
On trust in the state, the share of respondents who said the national economy had gotten worse rose from 31 to 48 percent. Negative economic evaluations are strongly associated with passivity, although the association weakens once other factors are taken into account.
The share who doubt Taiwan’s military could defend the island on its own rose from 69 to 74 percent. Confidence in the military and the expectation of U.S. intervention are among the strongest and most consistent predictors of lower passivity across every model. Passivity is highest among those pessimistic on both counts.
Finally, there’s trust in fellow Taiwanese. Respondents who believe “most Taiwanese would resist” are much less likely to opt to “let nature take its course.” Predicted passivity falls from about 36 percent among those who think their compatriots definitely would not resist to about 25 percent among those who think they definitely would.
The most important finding, however, is not the numbers themselves. It’s the breakdown of the survey results along political lines. Among respondents who identified with the KMT, expressions of passivity rose from 22 percent in 2024 to 40 percent in 2025, an 18-point jump. That difference holds after controlling for national identity, unification-independence preferences, confidence in the military, expectations of U.S. assistance, economic evaluations, and demographics. Among Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) identifiers, it rose from 26 to 30.5 percent, a change statistically indistinguishable from zero. The 13.6-point gap between the two trajectories is statistically significant.
I want to stress what this does not mean, because the finding is easy to misread. On its face, it might seem to show that KMT supporters love Taiwan less or are less willing to defend it. That’s not accurate. In 2024, KMT identifiers were actually slightly less fatalistic than DPP identifiers. In other words, at the start of Lai’s presidency, KMT supporters showed no sign of giving up on Taiwan’s defense simply because the DPP had won another term. 
In neither wave is the partisan gap on its own statistically significant. Both surveys took place under a DPP government, with KMT supporters in opposition throughout. The divergence between June 2024 and September 2025 therefore suggests that something changed over those 15 months in how the opposition camp relates to the DPP government. 
Between the two surveys, Taiwan went through more than a year of fierce executive-legislative conflict, ending in the 2025 Great Recall. Advocates framed the campaign to remove 31 KMT legislators as a defense of national security against Chinese infiltration. Opponents saw it as an attempt to overturn an election result. All 31 recall votes failed. The September 2025 survey was fielded weeks later. 
The partisan gap was already there. In both waves of the TNSS, KMT identifiers were about 20 points less likely than DPP identifiers to believe most Taiwanese would resist (roughly 61-63 percent versus 80-82 percent). In both the DPP and the KMT, the share who believe “most Taiwanese would resist” barely moved from 2024 to 2025. A substantial share of the electorate had already lost confidence that the burden would be shared.
But people’s own willingness to act did change, and it fell most among supporters of the KMT, whose political opponents had been presenting national security as a partisan cause.
Survey data cannot prove that any single event caused the shift. But when the language of national security becomes a weapon in domestic political combat, this pattern should come as no surprise. 
My reading is that the problem for Taiwan’s defense is not a lack of will but a lack of unity. It is very hard to ask citizens to risk their lives alongside people they already dislike and distrust in everyday politics, or to sacrifice for a government they see as a political adversary. The TNSS does not directly measure cross-partisan trust, so this interpretation needs further testing. It fits the evidence, though: a society that still sees itself as one nation but is increasingly unsure it can fight as one.
To gauge Taiwan’s willingness to fight, Sobol argued for watching behavior: recruitment, retention, reserve training, and civil defense participation. I strongly agree. I would add three sets of attitudinal indicators that come before this behavior and help explain it.
Do supporters of every party believe that the government asking for sacrifice governs fairly and competently, and that the country has a future?
Do citizens believe the burden is shared? Conscription reform, reserve obligations, and civil defense must be seen as universal, not selective. National security must stop being used against political opponents. Leaders of all parties should stop branding one another as Beijing’s proxies and should negotiate defense budgets and reforms as cross-party agreements.
Are allied signals consistent? Taiwanese must believe they can hold out until help arrives. Mixed messages from Washington or Tokyo damage the very pillar my data identify as most critical. Allies should also engage Taiwan’s major parties evenly, so that outside support is not seen as backing one camp.
These indicators should be broken down by party, age, gender, and region, and tracked across survey waves. If behavior and attitudes move together, across various segments of society, we can trust them more. If the aggregate holds steady while part of society quietly pulls back, we are looking at what I call “fragile resilience.”
articles.summary: Rising passivity in Taiwan doesn’t mean Taiwanese have given up on resisting. It means the conditions for political action are eroding.

articles.title: ‘Xi, You’re Not Welcome’: As Trump Hosts China’s Leader, Thousands Protest in Washington
articles.full_text:
Over 3,000 Tibetans, Chinese dissidents, Uyghurs, Hong Kongers, and other groups joined protests during Xi’s state visit, calling for human rights and political freedom.
Tibetan protesters hold Tibetan national flags and banners during a demonstration outside the Chinese Embassy against Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., on Sep. 24, 2026. The protesters called for a Free Tibet.
On September 24, more than 3,000 Tibetans gathered in Washington to protest Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House, in what organizers described as the largest-ever Tibetan rally in North America. The rally was organized by Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC) and supported by other Tibetan activist organizations.
The protesters came with demands that they said should be part of the China-U.S. relationship: that Trump raise human rights with Xi, that China release political and religious prisoners, and that Tibetans be allowed to preserve their language and culture. The group also demanded the repeal of China’s new Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, which took effect in July and promotes what Beijing calls a shared sense of identity among China’s 56 ethnic groups. Tibetan activists say the law further advances Beijing’s efforts to assimilate Tibetans into Chinese identity. Chinese authorities say the law protects minority rights while promoting ethnic unity.
“Human rights should not be left outside of their talks,” said Tencho Gyatso, president of the International Campaign for Tibet. “The Tibetans, the Uyghurs, the Hong Kongers, the Taiwanese, we want to make sure our voices are also heard there.”
The demonstration unfolded as Xi made his first state visit to Washington in more than a decade. U.S. President Donald Trump welcomed him to the White House for talks that touched on AI, trade, and other issues, while the two governments were also dealing with disputes over Taiwan, Iran and rare earths. Trump hosted Xi at a state dinner on the evening of September 24.
Outside, Tibetan protesters marched through the capital carrying Tibetan flags and signs reading “Xi Jinping is guilty of genocide” and “Tibet was never a part of China.” By the end of the day, the demonstration had expanded into a coalition that included Uyghur, Southern Mongolian, Chinese democracy, Taiwanese, Burmese, Falun Gong, and Chinese Christian groups, all people that have suffered under the Chinese Communist Party.
The rally began at about 9 a.m. outside the Chinese Embassy, where protesters gathered before marching toward the U.S. Capitol. Police were deployed around the demonstration as the crowd assembled. The protesters then moved through Washington, with Connecticut Avenue closed to accommodate the march. The crowd passed through Dupont Circle before arriving at the Capitol, where several speakers addressed the demonstrators.
Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat, joined the rally. McGovern called for human rights to be included in Trump’s discussions with Xi.
“No Xi in D.C. without human rights,” McGovern told the crowd.
He also criticized Republican lawmakers, who he said had declined to join efforts urging the administration to press China on human rights. “Are they afraid of Donald Trump? Are they afraid he’ll be offended if they ask him to ask Xi to release prisoners of conscience?” McGovern said.
Pelosi also spoke in support of the protesters, calling attention to human rights in Tibet and urging the release of prisoners of conscience.
For many Tibetan protesters, Thursday’s demonstration was also shaped by the death of Lobga Rangzen, a longtime Tibetan independence activist who died after self-immolating outside the United Nations in New York on July 2. Rangzen, 52, had called for Tibetan independence and unity in a final message before setting himself on fire.
Jigme Ugen, president of the Tibetan National Congress, said the size of the demonstration showed that the Tibetan independence movement remained active.
“This is the biggest gathering, as such, to not just protest Xi Jinping, but also to tell the world and the U.S. government that the Tibetan movement, and the call for Tibetan independence, is still very much alive,” Ugen said. 
Tsering Chomphel, president of the Tibetan Youth Congress, who traveled from India for the protest, said people had come from New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Philadelphia, Boston, Chicago, Vermont, and Toronto. “This is the first-ever mass gathering in North America. Whenever Xi Jinping or a Chinese delegation visits, TYC will be there to make sure our voices are heard.”
Seventeen Tibetans had set off on foot from the United Nations headquarters in New York on September 17, walking through Philadelphia before reaching Washington on the evening of September 23 – the same day Xi arrived. Rangzen Dolkar, one of the walkers, said the journey was meant to raise awareness about Tibet and Pawo Lobga Rangzen’s death. 
Pawo is an honorary title given to any individual who has sacrificed their lives through self-immolation to bring attention to Tibet’s situation. 
“I am a mother of two kids, and I left my kids home. We all took off from work and left on this journey,” she said. “People stop us on the way and ask us what we’re doing because they see the flag. It gives us an opportunity to speak about Tibet and what Pawo Lobga Rangzen sacrificed his life for.”
After the rally at the Capitol, the protestors marched to Franklin Park, half a mile from the White House, where speakers from the Uyghur, Taiwanese, Burmese, and Hong Kong communities addressed the crowd. 
Misran Dolan, president of the Uyghur American Association, framed the gathering as a common demand for political and religious freedom. “Free the Uyghurs. Free the Tibetans. Keep Taiwan free. Keep Hong Kong free. Keep China free,” Dolan told the crowd.
“All of us here have moved away from our homelands,” he said. “And now we’re here in the United States … to exercise those rights – freedom of speech, freedom of expression, freedom of religion.” About 200 members of the Uyghur community attended, according to Dolan.
The gathering also included Chinese democracy activists. About 50 members of the Democratic Party of China traveled from Los Angeles, according to Zheng Zhou, a member of the group.
“We want Xi Jinping to stop persecuting people. We want him to free Jimmy Lai, Ding Jiaxi,” said Zhou. Lai, the billionaire founder of Apple Daily, Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy newspaper, and a vocal critic of the Chinese Communist Party was sentenced to 20 years in prison earlier this February after being convicted of conspiracy to commit sedition and collusion with foreign forces. Marco Rubio, the U.S. secretary of state, had urged the CCP to grant him humanitarian parole calling the sentence unjust and tragic, 
Daniel Zhou, a Chinese Christian affiliated with an underground church – churches that operate outside China’s state-controlled religious system and whose members can face detention and other restrictions from authorities – spoke about the persecution of Christians in China.
“Our church leaders have to stay in Chinese jails, leaving their families praying and crying at home, just because they wanted to practice their religion peacefully in China,” Zhou said.
Cynthia Sun, a senior researcher at the Falun Dafa Information Center, said her friends from the United States had family members killed in Chinese prison through forced organ harvesting. “When they went to see their dead parents at the mortuary, their bodies were split open, there were stitches, and they were missing a heart or a kidney,” she said. 
Falun Gong is a spiritual practice that emerged in China in the 1990s and was banned by Chinese authorities in 1999. The Chinese government has been accused of forcibly harvesting organs from imprisoned Falun Gong practitioners. In 2019, the China Tribunal, an independent people’s tribunal, concluded that forced organ harvesting has occurred in China on a significant scale and that Falun Gong practitioners were likely the main source of organs. 
Sun described the persecution of Falun Gong practitioners as something that had followed her throughout her life. 
“I was born in July 1999, the month and year that the persecution began,” she said. “When I graduated high school, I thought the persecution would end by the time I got to college. But now I’m in grad school. I’m engaged, I’m getting married, and the persecution is still going on.”
articles.summary: Over 3,000 Tibetans, Chinese dissidents, Uyghurs, Hong Kongers, and other groups joined protests during Xi’s state visit, calling for human rights and political freedom.

articles.title: Trump-Xi Meet Again: A Summit Without Substance?
articles.full_text:
The visit’s outcomes are thin: a small extension of the trade truce and two pandas.
U.S. President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping of China arrive via the Cross Hall to a State Arrival ceremony on the State Floor of the White House, Sep.24, 2026.
In the latest episode of the Asia Geopolitics podcast, hosts Katie Putz and Ankit Panda are joined by Shannon Tiezzi, The Diplomat’s editor-in-chief, to discuss the outcomes – as we know them so far – from the latest Trump-Xi meeting, this time in Washington, DC. Xi’s state visit was heavy on vibes, as Tiezzi wrote in the aftermath, but light on substance. All the same, the meeting has implications for trade, tech, Taiwan, and more.
